Hon. FRANK OLIVER (Minister of the Interior) moved for leave to introduce Bill (No. 85) respecting Forest Reserves and Parks. He said: The House will remember that a Bill respecting forest reserves was passed in 1906. There was then in existence an Act respecting the Rocky Mountain park. The purposes of forest reserves and of forest parks, while identical in some respects, differ in other important respects. A forest reserve is withdrawn from occupation, whereas a forest park is intended primarily to be occupied for the purposes of pleasure. Since 1906 we have found that in many cases where a forest reserve was set apart, it was desirable that some portion, if not the whole of it, should be used for a park or other purposes. It has also been found necessary to increase the number of reserves, and that has been done by order in council. In other cases it has been found desirable on experience to cut out some of the reserves already made, or to alter their boundaries. This Bill provides a new schedule of forest reserves, which will be in accordance with the information we have acquired since 1906; and particularly it will include a forest reserve covering the eastern slope of the Rocky Mountains which was set apart last year by order in council. It was not included in the Act last year for the reason that the boundaries had not been defined. It is difficult to define the eastern boundary, and it was thought better that it should be set aparfmerely by order in council instead of by Act of parliament. Since last year we have had an examination made, and while we have not

been able to define the boundary for the whole distance on the eastern slope of the Rocky Mountains where it is administered by this government, we have been able to give what we think is a satisfactory eastern boundary, at any rate, as far north as the Jasper or Yellow Head Pass on the Grand Trunk Pacific line, and we are assuming a boundary from that point north. We think it is much better that, so far as we can define the boundary, it should be done by Act of parliament rather than by order in council. When we set apart a forest reserye by Act of parliament we take power in this Bill to apply certain provisions regarding parks, or parks in portions of this reserve set apart by Act of parliament, we take power to do this by order in council. The original reservation is made by Act of parliament, and there are certain provisions which cover that reservation. Out of that reservation there may be taken a portion which may be put under different regulations, so that the public may occupy that forest park for purposes of pleasure. One other new feature of the Bill is that we are providing powers of expropriation. In the present Act there is no power for expropriation of property which may be held by private individuals within an area that it is desired to make a forest reservation, or forest park. Sometimes we find a very serious difficulty in dealing with this question in the public interest, and we think it is desirable that a power of expropriation should be added to the existing provisions which provide for the purchase of existing rights either by payment or exchange.
Suppose a railway wishes to pass through this forest reserve, or suppose a person holds timber limits in what is set apart as a forest reserve, how is the minister going to meet that case?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Any rights that exist within the area covered at the time the park is set apart, are not intended to be prejudiced by the creation of the reserve. The holder of a timber limit still remains the holder of that timber limit, or the holder of private property still remains the holder of that private property. We are, as I say, taking powers of expropriation, not to expropriate such rights as timber limits or any Tights held by leasehold, but rights held by patent, those we take power to expropriate. In regard to railroads, if a railway runs by a certain route and that route includes a forest reserve, of course the park interest must give way to the paramount interest of the public in securing transportation.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

Mr. LEWIS moved for leave to introduce Bill (No. 86) respecting the carrying of offensive weapons. He said: This is a combination of a number of Bills that have been introduced in this House and in the English House. Those introduced in the English House have been law for some years. The Bill is entitled ' An Act to amend the Criminal Code respecting offensive weapons and capital offences.' It reads as follows:
It shall he the duty of every peace officer to search any person whom he has reason to believe is possessed of the weapon commonly known as a dirk or bowie knife, or any weapon resembling it, or which is not of a character or kind calculated to he used solely for an inoffensive purpose, or any weapon known as a pistol or revolver; and if any such weapon is found in possession of such person, the peace officer shall forthwith take him before the nearest justice of the peace or magistrate, who shall proceed to investigate the facts'and, if the accused is by such justice or magistrate believed not to be a native of Canada, he shall make a report to the Minister of the Interior in the matter, together with the evidence; and, if the said minister is satisfied that such person was an immigrant to Canada within four years previously, and had in his possession any such weapon, or if such immigrant is found within four years of his arrival in Canada in possession of any such weapon, the said minister may order the deportation of such immigrant, and section 33 of the Immigration Act shall apply to the case.	_

There is no one within reach of my voice who is conversant with what has taken place in Canada but will admit that there is reason for these amendments and that the government should deal with crime in a more forcible way than has been the case of late years. Formerly we could point with pride to our record with regard to criminal offences, while the reverse was the case in the great republic to the south of us. I have a number of newspaper clippings here with which I shall not trouble the House, but I shall merely refer to the head notes just to indicate what is happening in this Canada of ours. At one time the record of crime was very small in the whole of Canada. I am glad to say that in the maritime provinces and in the eastern paTt of the province of Quebec the former low average still holds good, but within the last three years the average of criminal offences in Ontario, Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta and British Columbia has more than doubled. That, Sir, is attributable, as one can readily understand, principally to the great importation of foreigners, and, secondly, to the fact that crime has not been punished with the vigour which formerly characterized the authorities. As I said, I shall not take up the time of the House by reading all these newspaper extracts, but I shall place before hen. members two or three items particularly with reference to the offences of Italians and to the practice of people of that nationality of carrying concealed weapons and of using them upon slight provocation.

The Bill also applies to revolvers. I introduced this Bill some years ago, and objection was taken to it by the sporting papers on the ground that it was going to curb the sale of firearms. But, I would say in answer that a revolver is not used for sporting purposes in any shape or form. The revolvers that these men procure are chiefly bought at second hand shops around the ports where they enter the country. The foreigner who comes in from Italy, Russia or southern Europe, where they have no such things as revolvers and are accustomed to the use of the stiletto, sees, first upon landing, a line of revolvers displayed in a second hand store, and thinking that in this wild, new country he will need something of the sort, purchases one of these weapons. The first clause of the Bill asks parliament to prohibit foreigners from bringing these weapons into the country, and it also calls upon the authorities to notify them that they cannot carry them, and that if they are found with weapons within four years after their entrance they shall be deported. I have notices here from nearly every city in Canada with reference to this subject. The first one that I have is from the city of Winnipeg. There is also one from Hamilton. The grand jury in the cit>
of Toronto made the following presentment:-
Cases of murder and manslaughter are occurring with alarming frequency. We are of opinion that many of these are the result of the carrying of deadly weapons. We submit that strong measures should be taken to prevent this dangerous practice. We respectfully urge upon the authorities the necessity of making it the duty of police officers and constables generally to search at any time such persons as might be suspected of carrying concealed weapons, and that the person upon whom such weapons are found shall be liable to imprisonment for a term of not less than three months without the option of a fine.
If legislation is necessary to the granting of such power to police officers and constables.

we recommend tliat the required legislation be sought without delay.
There is no reason why any one in this country should carry a revolver. Even if this Bill should pass there is nothing in it to prevent a householder from getting a revolver for his own protection. But, any one who takes the list of murders which have occurred in Ontario, Manitoba and the west within the last two years cannot but admit that it is necessary that some such legislation as this should pass. I have here a cartoon in which the whole matter is summed up. It represents a drug store and a hardware store. This appears underneath the picture of the drug store:-
The law forbids the sale of certain poisons without a physician's order. The law regulates the sale of all poisonous drugs.
Then, underneath the picture of the hardware store:-
Persons of suicidal or homicidal tendency supplied with murderous weapons; no questions asked.
Why should not the sale of revolvers be restricted the same as the restriction of the sale of poison? I quote a letter to the Editor of the Toronto ' Telegram ':

Sir,-The loose manner in which firearms are allowed to be displayed and sold in shops without proper restrictions speaks little for our boasted civilization. Accidents, suicides, murders, or some madman running amuck with a shooter make tragedies almost a daily occurrence.
The manufacture and sale of firearms should be entirely with the government of the country, their sale controlled by numbered license. This might do a lot to make crimes more detectable and restrain the needless carrying of firearms.
The government would do wisely to enact some measures rectifying the evil at the present session of parliament.
Here is an editorial article from the Toronto ' Star.'

The revolver is a small gun suitable for carrying in one's pocket, contrary to law. As a firearm it is not of much use except in committing murders, and in helping highwaymen and burglars to frighten their victims.
It is of no particular use to hunters. For birds, men use the shot gun, and for animals, the rifle. In time of war the revolver proves exceedingly useful when a man is at close quarters with the enemy, but in time of peace it is used almost exclusively in assassinations and accidents.
Yet these weapons are manufactured and sold by the thousands in a country that is always at peace-or would be except for tragedies and inquests. Why not suppress the revolver? Why not regulate its sale? Why not punish with ten times the present severity the crook who goes about among men loaded with the machinery for doing murder ?
Now, Sir, I shall read to the Housa certain remarks made by Judge Holt of the United States Supreme Court. He says :
The repeating pistol is the greatest nuisance in modern life. Every criminal, every madman, every crank, every had boy carries one. Nineteen-twentieths of all the crimes of violence that are committed are effected by its use. All firearms are weapons whose us* involves such terrible injury that no one should he permitted to use them except strictly in self-defence. Every person engaging in the business of selling revolvers should he licensed, and every person who wishes to obtain a revolver should he required to first obtain a license. It sbou'ld be a serious offense for a dealer in firearms to sell a revolver to a person who has not a license authorizing him to have it.
I submit, Sir, that this is one of the Bills which the government should allow to be sent to a conimittej which would include amongst its members a certain number of the members of this House learned in the law, so that there may be thorough inquiry as to the extent of the abuses which this legislation is intended to remedy.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

The chairman in moving the adoption of report and statement of accounts in March, 1910, said :
The more the committee had studied the subject the more vivid the prevalence of bribery came home to them. They found an amazing amount of corruption, some petty, some very serious.
Many employers considered their servants impeccable, while others did not care a jot what their servants did; but the public ought not to allow dirty things to go on in the servant's hall, the garden or the stable, any more than they would permit drunkenness or any other form of immorality.
Til sn, there is another reference here which might interest our Postmaster General. In the House of Commons on February the 20th, when a post office vote was under consideration one of the members stated with reference to mail carriers :
He felt that Xmas boxes were not only a tax on the public, but in his opinion it was a practice which lowered the British civil servants to have their salaries made up by touting around at a particular time of the year asking for gratuities.
Under the English Act, D. McLean was fined at Manchester 20 shillings and costs for giving a shilling to a carter of a railway company.
Now, Sir, the habit of tipping is a relic of the later middle ages. It arose from the masters wanting to give their serfs or servants small gratuities when they were sick or had large families, but which they were not entitled to. But when labour came to be organized and well paid and greater freedom prevailed, the practice of tipping went out of fashion. In Spain and Italy and other countries on the continent of Europe tipping is still so general that it is menial and impossible to do business without it. In England the same remark applies to the southeastern counties, where the farmers and people who live on a daily wage have not had their wages raised for over fifty years; but in the northern part of England, where labour is organized and men receive proper pay for their daily work, tipping has gone entirely out of use. In this country there are four classes to whom this Act will apply-waiters, coachmen, porters on railway trains, and barbers in cities. It has been recognized by the waiters' and barbers' [DOT] journeymen unions that where tipping is in vcgue men do not make as much as they would with a proper scale of wages. The barbers' union have started an organization to prevent tipping, and I will read to you the report of the secretary of that organization :-

Von Fleet, of St. Louis, of the Barbers' Journeymen's Union of America, says, making open war upon the tipping system:-

I detest this tipping system. It is base, wrong, unjust and degrading, and the barber who willingly accepts ' tips J simply does so by bowing in humble supplication to receive them, because he has done or intended to do work for which he cannot demand a recompense. It is practised and encouraged to such an extent that wages have been decidedly lowered. It is more manly to earn your living than to receive charity or bribes. Large tips mean small wages. Proper wages no tipping.
Now, Sir, we are founding a nation here, tlic last great nation of the wotM. We who are here are assisting to lay the foundations, and we look forward to the superstructure showing one of the finest national edifices in the world. We cannot hope to see the fruition of our desires, but every one of us can feel that we have a share in the honour of laying the foundation- The foundation of any country is the manliness, straightforwardness and integrity of its citizens, and I say without any fear of contradiction that any man in Canada who is able to earn his daily wage is degrading himself and his family if he takes from any one what he is not entitled to and what he cannot by law compel that other to give him. When the four classes in this country who take tips organize and are paid a proper amount for their services they will find that they make more money than they do under the present system. And, Sir, the poor man who wishes to travel with a fair amount of comfort, and who does not want to pay an excessive sum for his sleeping car, or chair car, or any other comfort, cannot get the proper attention unless he pays something in addition to what the railway asks. I say that the railway corporation should pay all that the man who gives the service requires for the service. Tips on ocean steamships are a great hardship and injustice. I bring in this Bill in all earnestness. There may be some people who think that it is straining a point, but even these will admit that it is better to work for fair wages than fawn for favours. But when we consider from what it arose, I think there is no one who will deny that it will tend to manliness and to make every Canadian citizen what we hope he will be and what the majority of them are-a man not a serf. ,
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time

Before the orders of the day are called, I would like to draw the attention of the government to the conditions now prevailing iii the Cobalt district owing to the dilatory policy of the Post Office Department. It is now nearly two years since the Temiskaming and Northern Ontario railway was completed to Cobalt, yet up to the present there is only one mail car running as far as
Englehart, which is 114 miles from Cochrane, the terminus of the Temiskaming and Northern Ontario at its junction with the Grand Trunk Pacific. At Kelso there is one bank, at Madison there is a bank, at Cochrane there are two banks, and at Porcupine five; and to show justification for my bringing this matter to the notice of the government, I might mention that at Porcupine alone there is laid the foundation for a great city.
I hope the hon. gentleman is not going into a discussion of the subject.

No, I only wish to justify my calling attention to it. All the money letters and others sent from Englehart north as far as Cochrane are at present simply thrown into a baggage car, which is a very loose way of handling such important matter. On the 15th December last I went down to the Post Office Department in order to press the necessity for a reform on the deputy Postmaster General, but he was ill at the time. I was, however, given to understand by his assistant that the matter would be taken up immediately, but until yesterday I heard nothing further about it. Yesterday I telephoned the department, and the assistant deputy told me that the deputy minister had gone west, and that nothing could be done until he returned, but that the deputy minister had given him to understand that something would be done. I would like to ask if, in view of the immense business done in that locality, whether it is not absolutely unbusiness like to allow such a condition of handling the mails to exist one day longer, and I would press on the government the necessity of having a remedy applied at once.

Has the attention of my right hon. friend the Prime Minister been drawn to a report said to have been made by the American section of the International Waterways Commission with respect to the project of damming the St. Lawrence opposite Cornwall canal for power purposes? I see by the Montreal
Gazette ' of this morning that this report of the American members of that commission is dated November 1, 1910, but that it did not see the light until to-day. Here is what I find in the ' Gazette ':
The commissioners, who had been instructed by the State Department to report on the subject, asked the co-operation of their Canadian colleagues, but the latter declined on the ground that they wanted more time to study it from a Canadian standpoint. The commissioners declare that the project, if undertaken, -should only be as a government work, or at any rate under complete government control.
It is entirely possible/ the report says, ' that a scheme of this kind, if, carried out under proper government control, would be of great advantage to both the United States and Canada, Under proper plans the navigation of the river might be improved, while a large amount of cheap power would be created and made available for use on either side of the boundary. The government must have such [DOT]control of the works after their completion as shall insure tlieir permanency and their proper manipulation in the interests of navigation. Its control must be so complete that it may be doubted whether it can be secured without actual government ownership. It is in the interest of civilization that the St. Lawrence river, where it forms part of the international boundary, should not go undeveloped, either for navigation or power. If [DOT]the two governments could unite in a scheme for canalizing it at the public expense the problem would be solved in a most satisfactory way/ The commissioners go on to say, however, that the United States government has its hands full now in other expenditures, hence this scheme would have to be carried out by Canada alone or by private capital. The Bill now before congress brings the latter alternative under discussion, and the commissioners suggest the inclusion of several clauses designed to secure government control. One of the clauses which they ask to have inserted provides that half of the power developed shall be delivered for use in Canada.
I have no comment to make-it would not be in order for me to make any comment on this report art the present moment. I desire, however, to know whether or not the Canadian members of the International Waterways Commission have had this matter under consideration and have made a report upon it. It was alleged here that they did not agree in the report of the American members because they had not had

time .to consider the matter from the Canadian standpoint. But the matter has been more or less before the public for at least a year, probably for eighteen months, and one would have thought that within that period of time they would have had an opportunity of taking this very serious matter into consideration and of making their views upon it known to the government. I desire to ask, in the first place, if the report of the American members of the Commission will be laid upon the table of this House. I think it important that we should have it. In the second place, I would put the question to which I have referred,- whether the Canadian members of the Commission have made any report, and, if not, whether they have had the matter undeT consideration. I would like to know also if the government does not consider it a subject that these gentlemen should take into consideration and report upon. And further, I would like to know whether that report will be laid upon the table of the House as soon as it is made.

has been received from the American commissioners upon this subject.
I am aware of that. They would make it to their own government.

I desire to call the attention of the Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid

Laurier) to a return brought down within the past day or two in reply to am Address of the House, dated 7th December, 1910, calling for a ' copy of all petitions, memorials, resolutions from individuals, boards of trade or other bodies and corporations favouring or asking for a treaty of reci procity with the United States;' (That is one branch.) ' And also all similar documents protesting against or unfavourable to the same.' (That is the second branch.) 'And a copy of all correspondence had with the government, or any members thereof, concerning reciprocity with the United States since the 1st of January, 1910.' I have in this return an answer-and I suppose a partial answer-to only one of these, that is, the documents and petitions in opposition to reciprocity. I find none at all reported in favour of reciprocity. That may be because no petitions have been sent to the government in favour of reciprocity. But I find it Tather difficult to believe that there has been no correspondence with any member of the government with reference to reciprocity with the United States since 1st January, 1910. I think there must surely be correspondence of that kind. The Order of the House covers that. I would like to have it looked into, to the end, that I might get a full return.
And there is another which is more important. I asked for, and the House acceded to the request, ' a copy of Sir John Thompson's memorandum, on the question of the rights of fishing in the bays of British North America, prepared for the use of the British plenipotentiaries at Washington in 1888, and a copy of the treaty agreed to and approved by the president.' I got a copy of the treaty, but I am told with reference to the paper prepared by Sir John Thompson that it is not on file in the department. It is inferred that it is a confidential memorandum, and therefore not in the records. I am loath to believe that the Dominion of 'Canada has not these records of firstrate. importance which were made in the history of the negotiations of the treaty of 1888. It surely cannot be that we have not in our archives an important paper such as this, prepared by the Minister of Justice of that time on the question of the bays and inlet3 in the controversy between ourselves and the United States. If it is not in our archives, somebody ought to be called briskly to account. Our archives are not worth a snap of your finger if we do not preserve in them these important state papers. As to the idea that it is a confidential memorandum, I do not suppose that it will be said that this is true now. It was not confidential even at that time; it was a matter in the negotiations at Washington, and both sides to the controversy were cognizant of it. It was a very important document, as I well remember. If it was not presented to parliament at the time negotiations were on, it at once dropped out of the category of confidential memoranda when the negotiations were over. I think this paper must be in the records, and I would like to have the attention of the Prime Minister to the matter.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: With regard to the first request of my hon. friend (Mr. Foster) concerning the correspondence which may have passed between the government of Canada and the government of the United States since January 1, 1910, I suppose the reason it was not included in the return is that the correspondence has already been laid before parliament. All such correspondence was brought down by my hon. friend the Finance Minister last session, and by myself, I think, at the opening of this session.
That is true with reference to the governmental correspondence, but not with regard to what was asked for.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: What is that?

Correspondence had with the government or any member thereof concerning reciprocity with the United States. Just as the government would receive a petition from a board of trade on the subject of reciprocity, so they might get a letter from John Jones giving his view on the subject. That is the kind of correspondence, and there must be heaps of it on file somewhere.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I thought that had been covered by the first part of the request.
No.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: What is the first part?
' All petitions, memorials and resolutions.' These are formal. The right hon. gentleman understands it now.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I will look into the matter. With regard to the second part of the hon. gentleman's request, relating to the memorandum of Sir John Thompson, I am not aware of such a record, but I will see if we have it. If it is not on file in the department, I agree, it should be in our archives. It may have been confidential at the time, but it has become historical, and there is no reason why it should not be brought down if it can be found.

Nevertheless, it is wrong, and the law of Ontario recognizes it as being against public policy, and makes it illegal to tax the people for any such purpose.
