Before you leave the Chair, I want to ask the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Pugsley) if it is his intention to place this session, in the supplementary estimates yet to be brought down, a sum sufficient to build and complete a wharf at the village of Brighton in the county of East Northumberland, the riding I have the honour to represent in this House. This is not the first time I have brought the Brighton wharf to the attention of the minister. At the outset let me say that the Brighton wharf is not a government wharf. It is a very old wharf, and it is in a very bad state of repair. It was built by a private individual, and has always been owned by a private individual, and the government have not expended one dollar toy way of maintaining that wharf. It is true that I have stood up in the House and pleaded for the good people in my riding, and I do not think it should be necessary for any member to humiliate himself as I have done, pleading on behalf ot the people of my riding that the government should expend a little money that is greatly needed there. I claim that we have a right to it. This wharf is not a citizens' wharf, it is not a village wharf, but it is greatly dilapidated, and a new wharf would be in the interests of the farmers. Now, Sir, the farmers of this county have seen the revenue increase from $40,000,000 a few years ago to over $100,000,000 last year ; they *have also seen the expenditure of this country increased during the last 12 years from a little over $40,000,000 to $140,000,000 last year, and they are wondering where that large amount of money has been expended. The farmers in my riding are wondering why, when the government are expending so large an amount of money, they cannot get a small sum of five or six thousand dollars to build a new wharf in my riding that is greatly needed. No wonder the farmers come here five or six hundred strong when they know that this govern-, rnent is expending to-day $15 for militia and defence, in time of peace, for every $1 it expends in the interests of agricul-

ture. _ No -wonder the farmers are coming here in large deputations to make known their wants, and I will go further and say, to make known their demands to the government. An hon. gentleman said here the other day, looking at the members of the Cabinet : You may be thinking what you are going to do with us, but you had better be thinking what we are going to do to you if you do not come down and grant our demands. Now, Sir, the farmer is waking up, he is beginning to understand these things, he is beginning to see that this government expended three-quarters of a million dollars in the province of Ontario in the interest of agriculture, while the Dominion government only expended about three-quarters of a million, in the whole Dominion of Canada, in the interests of agriculture.
_ It is true that a majority of the electors in my riding lean to the Conservative party, but I do not think they should be punished for that. I would hate to think that the Minister of Public Works is punishing the farmers in my riding because a majority of them vote Conservative. If a majority of them did not vote Conservative I would not toe here to-day, and I know the minister is glad that I am here. But, Mr. Speaker, I am sincere about this matter. This wharf is used largely by the farmers. The farmers in that community are greatly interested in growing fruit, and every season they ship largely over that wharf to the markets of Canada. Therefore, the farmers wonder how it is that the minister will not expend six or seven thousand dollars on this wharf, when he has built a wharf not over seven miles away at a cost of six or seven thousand dollars, in my riding, and never a boat has gone in there yet, although it has been built from three and a half to four years. Two and a half years ago previous to the general 'election all sorts of promises were made, and the Minister of Public Works sent his engineer down from Toronto to inspect the wharf at Brighton. He made a thorough examination of the wharf, and condemned it. Everybody thought the government was going to build a new wharf, and the engineer recommended to the hon. gentleman that a new wharf ought to be built at Brighton, but nothing has been done. Now, 1 hate to think that that work has been put off because I have been elected to come here, I would hate to think that the minister is punishing the farmers in my riding because a majority of them have voted Conservative ; I would hate to think that, and I will not make that- charge against the minister unless he says it is true. I must say this also, that there is not one government building in my riding. Here is a wharf that is greatly needed, that would be in the interest of the people in that riding, and also in the interest of the

people of the Dominion of Canada. Now i appeal to my right hon. friend the Prime Minister, and I ask him here, in all sincerity : Does he think that the farmers of my riding have been treated rightly, and are .being treated rightly by his government in denying them that wharf? I put the same question to the Minister of Public Works : Does he think that he is treating the farmers in my riding rightly in denying them a new wharf? It would only cost five or six thousand dollars, the resident engineer has already condemned the existing wharf, and two and a half years ago recommended that a new wharf be built.

The wharf to which my hon. _ friend refers is situated upon what is called Presqu' Isle bay. The harbour is a very capacious one, certainly it is a very excellent harbour of refuge. I have had the pleasure of visiting that harbour during the past season, and regretted very much that my hon. friend was not there. I should like to have shown him points in the harbour which attracted my attention. I am very glad to find that the hon. gentleman is waking up to the advantage of improving harbours and wharfs, and I trust that the spirit which he shows to-day may permeate the souls and the intellects of hon. gentlemen who sit around him, and that when I am asking for money to build necessary wharfs 1 may not. be charged with making large expenditures of public money, when perhaps it might be put to better use in other directions. I am a great believer, Mr. Speaker, in aiding the transportation of the country by building wharfs, and giving facilities to the farmers to get their produce to market. Now one difficulty about this wharf at Brighton Is, that it is a private wharf, it is owned by individuals, and when I was urged, as I was, by the gentleman who had the misfortune to be defeated by ,my hon. friend, to take over this wharf, it seemed to me that the price which the owners asked for it, was greater than I could recommend to my colleagues to pay for the property. I understand that now it seems to be apparent, that the property can be bought at a greatly reduced price from that which was first asked. I think I can say to my hon. >friend that, as a result of the visit which I paid to Brighton during the last season and the way in which I was impressed with the desirability of having improvements made there, if the wharf property can be turned over to the department at a low price, I should have much pleasure in submitting to my colleagues the question whether it shall be acquired, and the necessary improvements made.

Before you leave the Chair, I would like to ask the right hon. gentleman who leads the House and controls the government, when he is prepare 1 to lay before the people of this country for their information, and before this House, as, I think I may say, an apology to this House and to bis colleagues as a justification for his treatment of the hon. the Secretary of State, an explanation why that hon. gentleman has been inhibited from attending on this cheerful pilgrimage that has been undertaken to Washington. It is only a short time ago when the members of this House were asked by the Secretary of State, or the right hon. Prime Minister, to join in adding to-I will not say-the increased cost of living-buit to the expense of this government by subdividing the department of the government Which was supposed by every one who is at all conversant with affairs in Ottawa to he ithe department that of all others had the least to do. Since that time an inquiry has been carried on at the Department of Public Printing and Stationery and we had laid before ns a few days ago a most interesting blue book that shows that although there, was practically nothing to do in that department, it had most assiduously set itself to work not to do even that. Well, it seems that it was deemed necessary a short time ago, by an Act creating a Department of External Affairs, that such a department should be formed. This Act provided that:-
The Secretary of State as head of the said department shall have the conduct of all official communications between the government of Canada and the government of any other country in connection with the external affairs of Canada, and shall be charged with such other duties as may be from time to time assigned to the said department by order of the Governor in Council in relation to such external affairs, or to the conduct and management of international or intercolonial negotiations, so far as the same may appertain to the government of Canada.
The words of the statute would seem to be reasonably clear, but the right hon. gentleman who ied the House placed the meaning beyond peradventure in the explanation which he gave when the Bill was before the House. I will not read his remarks in full, but they will be found in ' Hansard ' of March 4, 1909, pages 1980-81-82. The right hon. gentleman pointed out that:
All governments have found it necessary to have a department whose only business shall be to deal with relations with foreign countries, and in our judgment Canada has reached a period in her history when we should follow the example of other countries in that res-

pect, as, for example, tlie commonwealth of Australia.
Then the right hon. gentleman proceeded to say that we had a Department of Interior for internal affairs, a Department of Marine and Fisheries for marine and fishery affairs, and that Canada, now having reached the status of a nation must, along with her sister nations, also have a department to conduct the external affairs of Canada. The House evidently relied on the argument advanced by the right hon. gentleman, and this Bill to create this department was passed. Now, within a year or two of the establishment of that department one of the most important pieces of negotiation that this government has attempted since it came into power-the reciprocity negotiations between this country and the neighbouring state-is undertaken. Although two ministers are deputed to visit Washington to negotiate with our neighbours, and although four of their colleagues find it convenient to be there at the same time, possibly to assist-at all events being there, they are able to assist-the one gentleman who apparently was constituted by parliament, to conduct these external negotiations, is the one who is left at home. I think it was the right of this House to expect, having acquiesced in the demand that such an office should be created, that when an opportunity for something to be done by this office, it should be done. Practically we find the office of the Department of External Affairs relegated to the position of a mail registering office. I suppose that any two or three of the pages who might not be occupied during the recess could discharge all the duties which apparently are the only duties which that department is considered competent to discharge; that is to file away the letters received from other departments, for surely, if the letters received by that department are answered by the department, then the officials of the department must have a better knowledge of what is going on touching matters referring to any such correspondence than outsiders. Therefore, it seems extraordinary that when the first opportunity occurs to give the department a chance to justify its existence we again have the old, old story, because when we come to test the reality of the promises made with regard to various expenditures by this government, and ask about them, the only justification we can get is that somebody got the money.
The hon. gentleman (Mr. Murphy) who fills the position of Secretary of State, I am sure, would not only have contributed to the success of the negotiations as far as Canada is concerned, but I am likewise sure, if I may judge from the interesting literature which he has laid before the Mr. NORTHRUP.
House in the last few days, that he could even have contributed to the gaiety of nations by his suggestions at such a time. If that hon. gentleman had gone to Washington with his colleagues, and if he had brought the same genial humour, the same sense of the eternal fitness of things, to bear upon our American cousins, who are proverbially fond of humour, as that which we find displayed in the investigation into the affairs of the Public Printing and Stationery Department, I am satisfied that most beneficial results would have followed. Who could have resisted the appeal that he might have made to our American cousins along the line of that which he addressed to the unfortunates who were brought before him in connection with this inquiry? If the House has any curiosity it can look at page 251 of this report.
Read it.

No, life is short, probably two hundred gentlemen will read it over more than once and they will get two hundred times the amount of satisfaction spread over two hundred times the length of time that they would if I were to read it but once. When we remember the hon. gentleman's wonderful sense of logic, I think it is unfair that the country should be deprived of his services at Washington. Just think of the irresistible effect that would be produced by such logic as that which appears in this report. When the report of that investigation comes before the House, as it will, I think it will puzzle the House to know what sort of description should be given to the bureau. Sometimes one would think it was the head office of the Shylocks and sometimes one would think that it was the head office, or a branch, of the Keeley Institute. Almost every possibility is covered by the reality in connection with that department. Of course, the hon. gentleman had before him the various foremen and he asked them to explain about the liquor that was used in the department and the most shocking tale seems to have been told when foreman after foreman had to admit that so many of his men were addicted to the use of the seductive beverage that one wonders, how any work was done at all. But the hon. gentleman was prepared to discountenance this and he laid down the rule again and again in the same terms that in the future it must be understood that any man who came to his work under the influence of liquor would be suspended for a week without pay, and that if he came a second time he would be dismissed from the department altogether. He displayed that keen sense of justice that I would like to have seen brought to bear upon the negotiations at Washington. In order that no one's feelings should be unnecessarily hurt, while impressing upon

the foremen that any man who came the first time under the influence of liquor should be suspended for a week without pay and should be dismissed for a second offence, he was careful to instruct the foremen, and to point out that this rule, severe as it was, should not apply to any one who did not use liquor. It is a pity that we should not have had the same logic, the same wit, the same humour, brought to bear upon these negotiations, for no one can tell now what will be the result of it. Therefore, I feel justified in appealing to the right hon. First Minister on behalf of the members of this House by whom he was influenced and to whom there is an apology due, for having induced them to pass this legislation which he, himself, has not only ignored, but made absurd and useless by declining to send the man to Washington whom he should have sent, and I also think that the right hon. gentleman should apologize to the nations of the world because the gaiety of nations has been so much decreased by the unfortunate absence of his colleague the Secretary of State from Washington.

I would like to ask the hon. Minister of Labour (Mr. King) whether the commission on technical education has completed its work. If it has not completed its work how much more lies ahead of it in the shape of visits to different places in Canada? Not very long ago the minister was able to state that the commission would pay a visit to northwestern Ontario and hold a session there. I see that although a requisition was sent to the commission no dates in Algoma have been fixed where there is a great deal of information along the line of that which the commission is anxious to obtain. I would, therefore, ask the hon. gentleman, if, the itinerary of commission has been completed why no sitting has been held in the town of Sault Ste. Marie, which the minister himself said was a centre in which that commission might obtain valuable evidence. If the commission has not completed its work will it hold a sitting at Sault Ste. Marie? If not, why not?

The chairman of the commission informs me that he has been in communication with the municipal authorities of Sault Ste. Marie and Steelton, and has made an arrangement about the commission visiting there. The commission has a very extensive field to cover, and it was the intention to visit Sault Ste. Marie early in December, but that could not be carried out. I understand the commission will go there some time during this month or in the month of February. I may say to my hon. friend that it is a little difficult to say how
long it will take the commission to com-piete its work. One part of its mission is to take evidence as to conditions in Canada, and the other to visit foreign countries and to see how needs similar to ours have been dealt with. The first part of the work has been about completed, with the exception of the visiting of a few localities. The commission is at present in Ottawa preparing a tentative interim report which will soon be ready. Its visit abroad will probably last several months, and on its return its final report will be prepared and presented.
Will the commission visit Sault Ste. Marie before it goes abroad?

I understand that to be the intention. When I was at Sault Ste. Marie I wrote to the chairman of the commission and he answered that three members _ of the commission would visit there. I replied that I thought it was important that all the commissioners should attend at Sault Ste. Marie. The chairman was unable to get all the members of the commission to go there before Christmas. He has, I understand, completed arrangements to visit Sault Ste. Marie with the full commission.

The commission has visited several places in southern and central Ontario, where the conditions are identical, and they have absolutely ignored the northern part of the province. I think I am safe in saying that between Orillia and Cochrane no point has been visited by the ccmmission, and it would seem as if it were mere a matter of personal convenience to them than of obtaining information with regard to the conditions in different localities; otherwise the northern portion of Ontario would have been given some consideration. In northern Ontario we have lumbering and tanning industries, and mining industries, and we have agricultural interests, with regard to all of which the conditions are different from those which obtain in the southern portion of the province. It would have been well had the commission held three, or four, or half a dozen sittings in northern Ontario.

It is largely left to the commission to decide as to what localities they ma\ desire to visit. The chairman of the commission has indicated to me that'if any members of the House feel that industrial centres in their localities should be visited, and will so inform him, he will endeavour to arrange that these localities should be visited before the commission concludes its work. The commission has had an eye to economy, and on that account some localities have not been visited, the commission believing that in the larger centres they might obtain sufficient information to guide them. I am quite sure the commission

wculd be glad to visit any locality where there is reasonable ground for believing some good purpose may be served by their doing so.

I have no apclcgy to offer to the House for taking up a little further time on the subject I have already spoken of. On December 14 I received the following letter from the superintendent of the Temiskaming and Northern Ontario railway:-
Mr. George Gordon, M.P.,
Parliament Buildings,
Ottawa, Ont.
Dear Mr. Gordon.
Would you mind calling upon the Deputy Postmaster General and ask him for a mail car to be run north of Englehart?
The amount of money going forward to the four banks in Porcupine, one at Hatheson, one at Kelso and two at Cochrane, as well as the individual letters containing sums of money, makes it of great importance that the mail car be handled north, and in charge of competent mail clerks instead of being put in our baggage cars as is now done.
Have asked the Deputy Postmaster General on several occasions to give this matter attention. Have written him, but lately have not been successful in getting any replies.
Would like to have you call upon him, and get some information for me.
Tours very truly,
(Sgd.) J. H. BLACK, Superintendent.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I have never gone to the Postmaster General to ask him for anything which was not in the interest of the district which I represent, as well as the country at large, nor will I ever do so. Here is something which should not be asked for, but which any ordinary business man would see for himself should be done at once. Has it come to pass that because the Postmaster General is absent from the country and the Deputy Postmaster General has been called away on business to another part of Canada, that the machinery of the Post Office Department must stand still? It is a matter of serious moment to have the enormous sums of money which are passing to and fro beween Englehart and Cochrane and Porcupine cared for in no better way than to throw them into an ordinary baggage car. I want to ask the government now if it is their intention to put a proper mail car on that route, and if so will it be dene at once?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Although the remarks of my hon. friend from Nipissing are somewhat heated, the House will be glad to hear that his district is improving so fast that the machinery of government is not equal to affording it necessary facilities. The Cobalt district is of comparatively recent development, and he, Mr. KING.
himself .has named several towns which a few years ago were not in existence and *which to-day are prosperous and doing a large business. He has told us that there are two or three banks at Cochrane and at other places along the line. That seemed to be a very good reason why that new section of the community should be served by all the facilities, postal and others, which the government can furnish for the diffusion of the ordinary knowledge necessary to its development. If that has not been done, I would be sorry to believe, as my hon. friend seems to imply, that it was through the negligence of the department. As he knows, the Postmaster General has been away, and will be here in a few days; and the deputy has been obliged to go to British Columbia on matters connected with the department, so that the force in the department is inadequate to deal with all requirements. But my hon. friend will perhaps believe that if the service has not yet been organized, it is not through any lack of good will or through any incapacity on the part of the government. . But my hon. friend knows that there aTe some rules on ttys matter. It is not sufficient that an application should be sent to the government to have it granted at once. My hon. friend knows that all such applications have to be looked into. The inspector has to be sent over the premises aid to make a report, and upon his report the minister or the department will decide. As my hon. friend attaches some importance to the matter, I will make it my duty at once to have inquiry made into it again, and on Monday, if it is called to my attention, I think I shall be able to satisfy him one way or the other as to the merits of the application to which he has referred.
Motion agreed to, and House went into Committee of Supply.

I would like to say, for the information of my hon. friend from the city of St. John, that in his absence last evening it was understood that under item '138 any question might be asked with regard to any public building in the maritime provinces.

I do not desire to ask anything very important. I wish to ask to whom has been awarded the contract <for the building of the drill hall, the price, when it will be finished, and whether the teontract will include everything that will be required for the building. In looking over yesterday's ' Hansard I notice that the minister stated that the contract would soon be awarded, but the Montreal ' Gazette ' contains a rumour that it has already been awarded.

I may say that I have signed a recommendation to council, but

it is not customary to give the name of the lowest tenderer until the contract has actually been awarded, and I would not like to depart from that rule in this case. J will not, however, deny the accuracy of the rumour my hon. friend refers to as having appeared in a Montreal paper. My understanding is that the contract will include all the fixtures-heating, wiring and plumbing. As to when the building will be completed, I am unable to state, because the contract has not yet been signed. The chief architect will report the time, that in his judgment, will be reasonably necessary to complete the building, and that time will be inserted in the contract.

As the minister states that the rumour published in the ' Gazette ' is Probably correct, the matter is practically concluded, so that I do not see that there is much object in keeping the information back any longer.

That is the rule. In
fact, it would be discourteous to His Excellency for me officially to announce that an order in council had passed until it has actually passed and has received His Excellency's signature. I can say to my hon. friend that if the order in council passes, as I assume it will, the successful tenderer iwill be invited to sign the contract immediately, so that the work will be proceeded with, with the least possible delay.

Another question I wish to ask the minister regarding the roadway and pavement at Fredericton. The amount paid by the government, including the vote passed yesterday, is stated in ' Hansard ' to be $4,800. What proportion does that bear to the whole cost of the roadway and pavement ? Is it half, or more than half, or less than half ?

It is one-half the total cost.
Artliabaska public building, $15,000.

This is to pay the contractor. Of this amount $10,000 is a revote. Pursuant to an appropriation last session, tenders were called for the work, and a contract entered into and the contractor is going on with it. The contract price is $22,000. The total cost of the building, in eluding the site and the fittings, furniture, lock boxes, sidewalks and fencing, is estimated by the chief architect at $34,500.
What is the size of the place?
The population in 1901 was given at 995.	[DOT]
What is the postal revenue?

The postal revenue is $2,334, money orders issued $10,300, money orders paid $18,937. Arthabaska is a shire town, and in addition to a commercial college, convent and hospital, contains quite a number of factories, also a tannery, two saw mills and a flour mill.
Was this put up to public competition?

Five tenders were received for the work, and the contract includes heating and electric wiring. I cannot say whether the fittings and letter boxes will be let by tender or not-probably not, but as far as possible we call for tenders.
Any clock in this building?
No.
What is the guide followed in building post offices. Does the postal revenue form a basis?

Usually the postal revenue is proportionate to the population, but not always. For instance a town which might be composed almost exclusively of residences would not have the same postal business as a business centre of the same population. The population and revenue, however, are elements which are considered. There may be towns which ordinarily would be entitled to public buildings, but which may enjoy sufficient postal accommodation. For instance the postmaster may have rented and fitted up a very suitable building, and thus the toifrn may have all the reasonable postal accommodation it requires. In such cases we would not consider favourably a request for a public building. There is no fixed rule, but, as I said the other day, we give in the first place more favourable consideration to a request from a shire town, as we rather recognize that each county is fairly entitled to one public building and prefer to give that building to the county town rather than to any other. But of course there may be exceptions because it may happen that a county town is not nearly as important as another in the same district.

Judging by the list of towns which are given public buildings, I should say that neither postal revenue, nor population is considered; but what I do notice is that in one of the Ontario towns where the hon. minister is building a post office, and which is represented here by a supporter of the government, the population is but 205. Yet he is putting up a building there to cost $15,000.
What town is that?
Tilbury.
Where does the hon. gentleman get his population?
From the census returns.
My hon. friend is wrong. It is one of the best towns in centre Ontario.
What is the population?
It is an incorporated town, so that its population must exceed 205.
What is the population?

Between 2,000 and
3,000.
The figures in the census must be a misprint.

Possibly, but in looking over the list, I find that the hon. minister has overlooked towns with three or four times the population, and five or six times the postal revenue of those where he is building post offices, and in these larger towns he is not doing anything. But practically all these small places on which he lavishes his gifts, are represented by government supporters.

The hon. gentleman makes a general criticism, and a general criticism is easily made. But when an item comes up for a public building in a particular town, if the hon. gentleman ia sincerely of the opinion that a public building should not be erected there, he ought to vote against it. I do not find, however, that he voted against a public building, even for the town of Tilbury, although he thought its population was "only 205.
What effect would that have?
It would put him on record as opposed to that particular public work.
But what effect would it have on the government?

One never can tell. Does my hon. friend not think that after all that would be much more effective criticism than this general condemnation. The hon. gentleman made a general criticism and then he instanced one place which he thought only had a population of 205, but when he found that its population yras between 2,000 and 3,000, of course he had nothing more to say. No doubt there are many places which might fairly be entitled to a public building. In many cases there may be one or two buildings in the same county. Or it may be that the town already has good postal accommodation. I have in mind one case. Application was made to me by a delegation from a very thriving Mr. LALOR.
town in the province of Ontario. They said : We are at the gateway of a splendid country through which many thousands of tourists pass every year, and it would be a fine thing if we could have a public building in which we could take pride and which our people would be proud to show to visitors. 1 was favourably impressed. But afterwards it was represented to me that while it would be nice to have a public building there it was not absolutely required in the public interest. The postmaster at an expense to himself of about $1,200 had provided a building and fitted it up very nicely for the accommodation of the public, and it was represented that if we put up a public building he ought to be reimbursed for his expenditure.
What county?
In Muskoka.
Ah !
What's the matter?
The hon. gentleman (Mr. Pugsley) knows what's the matter.

No. I am sure the hon. gentleman will not criticise that position. I have a vote for a fine wharf on Lake Muskoka in the district represented by the hon. gentleman sitting opposite me (Mr. Wright). I hate to tell how many things I am doing for constituencies represented on the other side for fear my friends on this side may feel that I am doing almost too much for these gentlemen. My friends on this side are very patient ; they do not abuse me because I cannot do everything in' a day or a year ; they are willing to wait reasonably for public expenditures. I try to meet their views as rapidly as possible, and I hope I shall be able to meet the reasonable expectations of their constituents. We do not limit expenditures to constituencies represented on this side of the House, and I am sure the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Blain) does not mean what that ' Ah ' would imply.
The hon. gentleman (Mr. Pugsley) soon gathered what it did imply.

It seems to me that the system adopted by this government in regard to public buildings is absolutely corrupt and degrading. Perhaps, I should say 53J
the want of system, for there seems to be no system except that of strengthening the government's hands in the various constituencies. Yesterday, we had the case of a large expenditure being made in a little village of seven hundred inhabitants, though you could find a score of towns in the province of Ontario that are more important that have no public building. To-day, we have a proposition to expend a large sum of money in a little village of 900 inhabitants in Arthabaska. The figures have not been given us, but I fancy that the net revenue from these places is very small, if there is any net revenue at all. Now, I hold that a rule or principle ought to be laid down by the government as to the circumstances in which a public building will be erected. When these circumstances are met, when the rule made or the principle adopted is complied with, then the building should necessarily go up. It is obvious to every member of this House the system or want of system followed by this government is a degrading and a corrupting influence on the people of this country. They see a little place like Hartford down in Nova Scotia, with 700 inhabitants, getting $16,000 for a public building. People say, the government is spending millions, and we might as well get a part of it as some other place, and then they ask their member to get as much money as he can out of the government for their little village or town. The member is actually forced to come to the Minister of Public Works, and upon his knees to beg of him to spend a few thousand dollars in his little town, when the expenditure could not be defended upon the around of principle or the ground of public necessity. I say it should not depend upon the fact whether a constituency sends a supporter of the government here or a gentleman in opposition to the government. This lack of system has been going on for years and years, and is exercising a corrupting influence upon the people from ocean to ocean. It is high time that it should be stopped, that some principle should be adopted, that some rule should be laid down, and when the officers of the department determine that these conditions have been met, then the public building should go up as a matter of right, if there is money in the treasury for that purpose. If there is not enough money, then the places where the specified conditions exist should take their turn. Now I hope that verv shortly we shall see an end of this log rolling here for improvements of this kind) and that a man should not be (Tenied a necessary improvement because he cannot bring to bear the necessary political influence. At present we see deputations waiting upon the Minister of Public Works begging him to do this or that for their little town or village and if sufficient political pressure can be brought to bear

upon the minister the request is granted. Yesterday we had a little town thirteen miles from the shire town-my hon. friend throws that in at every opportunity, that it is a shire town. Well, we had a little place down in Carleton, thirten miles from the shire town of Woodstock, a little village of 700 inhabitants, getting an expenditure of $16,000, with no justification whatever for it. It is high time such expenditures should cease.

As the minister has seen fit to mention the deputation from a town I represent, I gather from what he said that he does not intend to comply with the views of the deputation from the town of Bracebridge, on account of the postmaster having made some improvements there.

No, I said that representations had heen made that the postmaster was providing a very good accommodation at a considerable expense, and that a public building is not immediately required.
I did not say what conclusion I had reached on the subject, because the matter is under consideration.

I may say to the minister that I am personally acquainted with that town, I am personally acquainted with the postmaster, and cognizant of the conditions of the post office. The postmaster has done the best he can fox the public with the limited space at his disposal, but the post office even to-day is not up to the requirements of the town. It is an important town, what the minister terms a shire town, yielding a revenue of over $7,000, a much laTger revenue than is afforded by dozens of other places that are being supplied with public buildings. We have not a public building in the district of Muskoka oi any kind. It is true that the minister has been promising a wharf, and I hope he will proceed during the coming season to erect it. It has been promised now for a good many years, we have had' votes from time to time, and I am looking forward to the time when these prc mises will be fulfilled. I hope the minister will put up the wharf that he has promised there. At the same time, I may say that I think the district of Muskoka, which is pretty well settled, a very large district, with three towns in it, having a postal revenue of over $5,500 each, should receive better consideration, and that these places should be provided with public buildings, if it is the policy of the ministei to go on with the erection of public buildings throughout the country. I have long been of the opinion that there ought to be some system laid down with regard to this matter, that, for instance, the towns with the largest postal revenue should first be provided, no matter in what nart of the Dominion they are to be found, and so on ^ down the line. In that way public build-Mr. CKOTHERS.
ings would be erected in important centres where the revenue from post office and customs warrant it. If that system were laid down and followed, I cvould make no complaint on behalf of my riding, knowing that it would receive consideration in its proper turn. At present it does seem to me that some important towns are being side-tracked *without justification. I think the Minister of Public Works might adopt some system in concert with the Postmaster General, who should say to the Minister of Public Works where a post office ought to be erected, and that the system should be brsed upon the gross revenue derived, unless there is some special reason to the contrary.
Aylmer post office, $3,000.

This is for the purpose of making certain improvements to the post office at Aylmer, in the province of Quebec. We propose erecting an addition of two stories, and the contract is actually let. The total estimated cost will be $6,000, according to the chief architect. It is an extension to the present building.
What did the present building cost?
The total expenditure on the present building up to the 31st of March, 1910, was $18,184.51, of which $4,997 have been for repairs.
I have been there, and I noticed that the building seemed to be a pretty good one for the size of the place. I am curious to know why it needs enlarging in view of the size of the place.

Let me say a word, as this is in the county I represent. This building was erected when Sir HectoT Langevin was Minister of Public Works, and there have been practically no repairs made to it for about 17 years. At the back of the building there is a kitchen, which was very badly built, a building of one low stcrv, in which it was impossible to live during the winter time. Repairs here are absolutely needed. Some of the first persons to bring the matter to my attention were good, staunch Conservatives in the town of Aylmer, and it has absolutely no political significance.
The statement of the hon. gentleman is different from that of the Minister of Public Works, and I would not have made any comment had the minister said what the hon. gentleman has just said.
He said just the same.
The minister said that it was extending the building.
There is an addition.
Well, it is extending the building, it is not repairing an old building, and I want to know what it is?
It is really both.

That is not what the hon. gentleman said. He said that it was
because the building had been improperly built and the kitchen behind it. I did not know that post offices and kitchens were associated. Perhaps it is a soup kitchen, I do not know what it is. However, as the member says it is a matter of repairs, and the minister said it was an extension, it seems to be both. I want to know how much is new building, and how much is repairs to the old building?
Was that voted last year?
Yes, this is a revote of $3,000.
What is the amount to be spent?
The total estimated cost is $6,000.
What was voted last year?
$5,000 was voted last year.
Has any work been done?
Yes, we will have expended up to March 31, $2,000 upon the work, and we are only asking for a revote now of $3,000.
What is the population of Aylmer?
It is over 2,000 and in the summer months about 3,000.
Why did my hon. friend allow this building to go to rack so long?

Had it been properly constructed in the first instance it certainly would not have required these additions, but it was constructed by Sir Hector Lan-gevin, and the architect employed by the government-I am not sure whether Mr. Ewart was there then-may not have been as expert as they are to-day. I_am not in the habit of asking the government to expend any money upon public buildings unless I am assured it is absolutely necessary, and I can assure hon. gentlemen that this is money which is properly required for the repair of the building.
Here is a building that was constructed many years ago. My hon. friend was hoping to be able to complain against the former architect but he finds that it is the same architect.
No, no, the contractors.

Here is a building that has required repairs for so many years. Last year they asked for $5,000, and now they are asking for $6,000. It appears to me that if the hon. gentleman had taken care oi the public interest this building would have-been repaired some years ago, possibly at a cost of $2,000. It took my hon. friend about:, fourteen years to find out that something had gone wrong under the old government,, and now he is going to cure it with an expenditure of $6,000.

It seems to me that it would be well for the minister to give us some further details as to how he proposes to expend this $6,000 because it will go out to the country that he is expending this $6,000 to repair the caretaker's kitchen. Most of us are unable to get -a whole house that is worth that. It would look rather -bad to have it appear that they were fixing up a kitchen at an expense of $6,000.

There are the repointing of the building and general repairs. I think the best I can do is to charter a Hull electric, car and invite my hon. friends out, because I can then point to the necessity of -this work.

I can tell the hon. gentleman that without his chartering any .cars some of his friends had the curiosity to go out there years ago, and one of the first things that struck them was the enormous size of that public building compared with the sparse and meagre population of the town. If such towns were given a post office in proportion to population and revenue $6,000 would build the whole public building and not merely repair the caretaker's dining room and kitchen and install some electric lights. The hon. gen, tleman may not have said anything until

he thought it was necessary, but when he did say anything to the government he seems to have got in one chunk about ten times more than was necessary to provide for the propeT carrying on of the public affairs of the town.
What was the original cost of the building ?

There has been expended on construction $18,184.
Dominion public buildings-renewals, improvements, repairs, &c., $20,000.
This is the usual vote for public buildings in Quebec.
How much of the vote was spent last year ?
Would not the item for the town of Aylmer naturally come out of that vote ?
No, that would be too large.
Is this amount of $20,000 spent in small sums ?

Yes, running from $15 up to $2,600. They are small items extending over thirty or forty different buildings.
Grosse Isle quarantine station-improvements and repairs to buildings and fittings, furniture, &c., $7,000.
These are asked for by the Minister of Agriculture.

I notice an expenditure at this point last year. My hon. friend will find at page V-36 of the Auditor General's Eeport
Emond, V. A. & Son: 4-in. water filters, 2 at $700 ; connections for same, $475-$1,875.
The Minister of Agriculture perhaps could explain as to that.

These are quite large, expensive and complicated machines which are required to purify the water at Grosse Isle for the patients in the hospital and were ordered under the direction of Dr. Montizambert. I was surprised myself at the cost of them, and when I came to look into it, I found that there were no other machines that could be obtained. These could not be obtained at any lower price and when one sees the machines he can easily understand that they cost as much as they do.
Where were they made ?
In Montreal, I think.
Did you invite public competition for them ?
There is no competition; they are a patented article. The physicians in charge of the department recommended them as being the only ones useful for the work.
Is the only filter made in Canada made in Montreal?
The only one of that character.
Where is the water supply for Grosse Isle obtained?
It is St. Lawrence water which at that point is brackish.
Is the drinking water taken from the St. Lawrence river?
I am not positive whether the drinking water is not obtained from a well.

I understood the minister to say that this filter was for the purpose of filtering the water for drinking purposes. If that water comes from the St. Lawrence it would have to be distilled, and would not need to be filtered.
I don't think that water is used for drinking purposes, but I would not be positive. I think the filtered water is for the general supply of the quarantine station.
Was there any filtering system prior to this?

I cannot remember.
Grosse Isle quarantine station-new buildings, $50,000.
The Minister of Agriculture can give information as to this.

Last year one of the buildings which was about 40 years old caved in from the weight of snow on the roof. That building was used only in emergency, but its disappearance decreased the accommodation. Wj had had representations from agents of the shipping companies that the passengers complained of the character of the accommodation at this quarantine station, and having made a special trip to the island to investigate I felt that these complaints ware justified. The Grosse Isle buildings were erected 30 or 40 years ago at a time when the accommodation on passenger ships was of a very inferior character, and no doubt the quarantine accommodation was equal to the needs of the time. But, in the past 30 years the accommodation for ocean passengers on the ships has improved wond?rfully, and the accommodation on the island was certainly not commensurate with the accommodation now provided on the ships. I also found that the accommodation at Grosse Isle was -inadequate. On one or two occasions we had 2,000 people detained there,

but fortunately it was in summer, and in some cases we were able to accommodate them in tents. What we purpose doing is to use the old first-class building as a second-class building, and to erect a new first-class building as well as a third-class building of a standard suitable for third-class passengers. By the erection of these two 'buildings and some improvements in the existing buildings I think the accommodation will be sufficient for present needs. I had a report from Dr. Montizam-bert, Director General of Public Health and a special report from the officers at the station as to not only the desirability but the absolute necessity for this expenditure.
What was the size of the old building which fell in?
Speaking from memory, it was a low, wooden building, 100 by 24 feet, and the walls 8 or 10 feet high.
Could it not have been repaired?
No, the foundations and the walls were rotten as well as the roof beams which gave way.
What is th3 size of the new building?
The first-class 'building is of two stories with an attic and basement, 22 feet by 152, with kitchen in the rear' and two small (buildings adjacent to be used for a laundry and a bakery.
It will afford twice as much space as the old building?
Threa times I should say.
What is the total cost to be?
Of what material is it to be built?

It is to be of brick with stone or concrete foundation walls, copper roof covering, and iron stairs with slate treads, good heating apparatus, and a bakery and laundry. The old buildings were all wood. The staterooms are to be supplied with all the conveniences to be found in corresponding rooms on the best lines. We have to supply what we ought to have had long ago, fire escapes on all buildings of two stories or more. This building is to have two stories. We have to make some changes to meet the demands of second-class passengers.
I suppose you have a fire protection service there?
Yes, we have a hose, a pump and a hydrant.
Has the contract been let for this building?
Not yet. The plans are now in course of preparation, and we expect to call for tenders in the early spring.
I ought to say that the estimate of the architect's branch is that the cost of this building will be about $40,000.
There is another building proposed to be built besides this one?

Yes, a third-class building. That will be of wood. Its estimated cost is about $3,000.
Levis-armoury and gun shed, $30,000.

This is to make provision towards the erection of a drill hall in the city of Levis. The site has been provided by the municipality free of cost to the government. It is on St. Antoine street between St. Louis and St. George streets. The building is to be two stories high, built of brick with stone dressings on a stone foundation. It will be 112 feet by 103 feet, exclusive of a small projection on the southwest corner. There was a vote last session of $20,000, and we are asking for a revote of $19,000, so that very little has been spent.
What is the total cost to be?
The chief architect estimates the total cost at $100,000, including the fittings.
When is it proposed to build it?
The plans are finished, and we expect to call for tenders very shortly.
Has there been a drill hall or armoury there before?
I think not.
What quantity of troops are there requiring it?

This is the information given to us by the Department of Militia and Defence. The 6th Regiment of Artillery is there; they say they have no guns because they have no accommodation. The full strength of the force is 265 officers and men. Then there is the 17th Regiment, with 196 officers and men.
How did these two forces get along without a building up to the present?

I understand from the hon. member from Levis that they have

been suffering a very great inconvenience. I think they have been storing their arms and equipment in a rented building.
When was the money for this building first voted?
I think in 1907-8.
Will the hon. minister tell us why, if there was so much need of a building, nothing has been done about it.

As early as 1906 the Militia Council made an application for a drill hall at Levis, and a vote was taken as early as 1907-8; but there was considerable delay caused by a difference of opinion as to what would be the best site for the building. A site was proposed at first, which was disapproved of because it was thought a better one could be got, and finally the town agreed to give the present site, which is a desirable one, and approved by the militia authorities.
When was the present site decided upon?
I think during the past year.

The minister said the same thing a year ago. He said this:
The site is being provided by the municipality of Levis free of cost to the government.

Of course, I cannot keep the details with respect to all these buildings in my head; but I remember that there was a good deal of negotiation between the town and the Militia Department carried on by the hon. member who represents Levis as to the giving of the site and as to whether the town should insist on certain conditions as to the character and cost of the building. There was a good deal of negotiation, and it is only recently that all these matters have been settled.

If this building were needed four years ago, the government were very remiss in not putting it up, and if the people could get along four years without it, it is questionable whether it is really needed to-day. It seems to me that the Minister of Militia ought to be here when an item of this kind is up. We are in the dark, and I am sure the Minister of Public Works is not in a position to enlighten us from the point of view of the militia requirements.

I can say what probably the Minister of Militia would say, and that is that as early as-1907 this was pressed on the Public Works Department by the Militia Council. I have had a great many conversations about it with my hon. friend from Levis (Mr. Carrier), and he has urged the necessity of this drill nail very strongly. Over and over again he has called my Mr. PUGSLEY.
attention to the inconvenience from which the regiment is suffering in not having a drill hall. My hon. friend knows that in 1907-8, when there was a period of depression and our revenues declined, we had to let many important public works stand over, and this was one of them.
This is one of those peculiar cases in which the government seems to insist that a municipality should purchase the site for a building. What principle, if any, governs the minister in these matters?
The department never stipulates that a municipality must furnish a free site.
But they accept it.

The town in this case offered the site and we accepted it. Of course that is some inducement to the department to move a little quicker and perhaps put up a better building, but we always decline to stipulate as to the class of building, and we never make it a condition that the town must furnish a free site. That would not be fair because the government can afford to pay for a site when it needs cne, but 1f the town offers a desirable site, I would not be doing my duty if I refused.

The system is a pernicious one. It is just as bad when a free site is offered as when you insist upon being given one. The fact of the government accepting free sites causes the people to believe that they are more likely to get a public building if they offer the site. In the city I have had the honour to represent, as part of my constituency, eleven years, after I was here a couple of years I found it was absolutely necessary for St. Catharines to have a drill hall, and I was told by the minister of that day, the late Mr. Tarte, that if I could get the municipality to furnish a first-class site, the department would put up the building, but that otherwise it would not. I am not saying that that is the rule followed, but the people are not to be blamed if they conclude that in order to get a drill hall they must furnish the land. I think the principle is a bad one. Either the building ought not to be erected at all or the government ought to be able to pay the whole cost. If the public service requires a building, the site should be paid for by the government and not be made a tax on the municipality. In St. Catharines, we had to pay $6,500 for the site selected by the Militia Department. I am not saying that the militiamen of that locality are not well served, on the contrary they have a first-class drill hall, and no one is complaining, but where a public building is required for the public service, the municipality should not be taxed to provide the site. It

might be a different thing If the municipality owned the land, and had no particular use for it, but the people of the municipality should not be specially taxed to pay for a site and hand that over as a gratuity to the King as represented by the Dominion parliament. There is another reason against this course and that is that it causes discrimination. Either every municipality which is given a public building should contribute the site or none should be called on to contribute.

In this particular case,
I understand the town of Levis was the owner of this property.
What about the principle ?

I would never make it a condition of the erection of a public building that the municipality should give the site; but I am not quite so far advanced that, if the municipality offered the site,
I would consider it my duty to refuse it. There is Regina, for instance with a splendid block of land admirably suited to be the site for a drill hall and armoury. The city owns that block of land. They have volunteered that, whenever we want to erect an armoury and drill hall in Regina, they will make a free gift of this well situated piece of property to the government for that purpose. They got it free some years ago, and they offer to give it to the government free as a site for a drill hall and armoury. In the case of Port Arthur, when I was there last summer, the mayor and a number of prominent citizens, told me that the town would give the government so many thousand dollars toward purchasing a site for an armoury. My hon. friend from Thunder Bay and Rainy River (Mr. Con-mee), was present and he will remember what my answer was. I said: If the town chooses to make a donation of an amount of money to pay for the site, well and good; we shall be glad to receive it; it will show that the town is interested in securing an armoury; but I can assure you, Mr. Mayor, that that will make no difference; we do not ask you for this contribution, and you can give it or not as you please, but it will not affect in the slightest degree the action of the department in relation to this drill hall and armoury.
Is it to be constructed?
We have an appropriation which we shall come to as one of the Ontario items.

Perhaps the minister has not understood me. I want to point out that, by the law of Ontario-I do not speak of other provinces, though I fancy a similar law exists in others-it is really illegal for a municipality to do what St. Catharines had to do to get that building.
And, had any ratepayer taken action to quash the by-iaw taxing him for this $6,500,
I believe he would have succeeded in the courts.
I suppose the town felt seme little pride

The people of St. Catharines wanted this building, and the man would be very unpopular who would ir.voke the law to prevent an expenditure ol $6,500 of civic money which would result in obtaining a public building costing $90,000 or more. Nevertheless, it is wrong, and the law of Ontario recognizes it as being against public policy, and makes it illegal to tax the people for any such purpose. That is the reason why I recommended the minister to consider whether he ought to accept these contributions. He cannot but see that it is apt to give rise to competition between municipalities for drill halls and other public buildings. One municipality might be the proper place for such a building, but the other municipality might say: We will get ahead of our rival by getting our lepreientative to offer the Dominion government a site. Such a thing ought to make no difference whatever, and I think the best way to settle it would be for the government to say: We wall insist on paying a reasonable price for the land upon which a public building is to be constructed.
At six o'clock, House took recess.
After Recess.
House resumed at eight o'c'ock.

On section 2,-time for construction of branch lines extended.

subtopic: THE BRITISH COLUMBIA SOUTHERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext:
There was a remedy suggested in the committee, which I think ought to be in future Bills of this kind. There are several branch lines to be commenced, then w'e say that if they are commenced within two years and completed within five years, the requirements of the Act will be complied with. Now, if I correctly understand it, provided they commence the construction of any one of these branch lines, it would mean the commencement of the whole of them. It seems to me when branches are set out that way, it ought to be provided that there must be a commencement of each one of them to comply with the Act. In

the case of another Bill, after it was passed, we did make that amendment, and it seems to me this one ought to be amended in the same way.

subtopic: THE BRITISH COLUMBIA SOUTHERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: We discussed that question in the committee, and the chairman was inclined to the belief, along with the clerk, that the wording in the Bill itself would cover that point. It refers to branch lines in the plural; it says ' if the said branches are not so commenced.' If only one of them is commenced it would only apply to that one. The hon. gentleman brought that question up in the committee, and the chairman said that he thought this covered it.

subtopic: THE BRITISH COLUMBIA SOUTHERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: No, the committee decided to change it and amend it in that direction.

subtopic: THE BRITISH COLUMBIA SOUTHERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: That was not my understanding.

subtopic: THE BRITISH COLUMBIA SOUTHERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: I think it was at the suggestion of the minister or the clerk that it was read in that way. That provision is in another Bill, and I think the same principle is involved in both.

subtopic: THE BRITISH COLUMBIA SOUTHERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: ' Such branch lines as are authorized by the Governor in Council shall be commenced.' It means they must all be commenced within two years and completed within five years; and if such branches are not so commenced or not completed and put in operation within the said periods respectively, the powers of construction conferred upon the company shall cease with respect to so much of the branches as remain uncompleted. It seems to me that the plural being used, such branch lines shall be commenced,' it would not be a compliance with the terms of the section if only one was commenced.

subtopic: THE BRITISH COLUMBIA SOUTHERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: That is where the difficulty comes in. I do not pretend to put my opinion against that of an eminent lawyer, and say that it would be in strict compliance with the Act to commence only one of them. What I say is that if this language is not plain enough to cover that clearly then we ought to remove anv possible doubt.	*

subtopic: THE BRITISH COLUMBIA SOUTHERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: This matter was brought up in the Railway Committee when my hon. friend (Mr. Sproule) advanced the same idea as he has just now. But the committee decided, I believe, that the Bill should pass in the form m which it was printed, and consequently no change was made. The committee was satisfied with the Bill as it was, and did not countenance any change, even although it was pointed out by my hon. friend that there might be a little inconsistency.

I was sitting in the committee, and distinctly understood that the language was to be changed.
