We purchased a site first from Mr. Morgan of Montreal, and subsequently it was represented to us that we could get from him in exchange a considerably larger piece of land which would be adjacent to the proposed public park and we made the transfer.
How long did the government own the land?
Only a short time. We paid $8,437 for the site. We got in exchange for it a property 100 x 125 feet on Ontario street. The estimated cost of the building will be $40,000.
What post office have you there now, and what rent do you pay for it?	-

We have a rented building for which we pay $60 per annum, but the new building will b^ a postal station. The present accommodation is utterly inadequate. It is a portion of the city of Montreal which is growing very rapidly.
Is it a portion of the city of Montreal at all?
Yes, for all practical purposes, it is immediately contiguous to the city.
What is the population?

A few years ago it was
4,000,	but I presume it is 20,000 now.

Last year there were many outside municipalities annexed to the city of Montreal, and although Maisonneuve is not annexed yet the territory further east at Longue Pointe, and to the north, is now part of the municipality of Montreal, so that Maisonneuve is practically surrounded by the city. My hon. friend from St. Anne knows that.
Maisonneuve does not form any part of the city of Montreal, but it is surrounded north and east and west by the city.
And south.
It is bounded by the river on the south.
Maisonneuve is now about in the centre of the city of Montreal.

There is a central post office in Montreal, and if Maisonneuve is in the centre of the city as the hon. gentleman from Laval states, Maisonneuve must be within a reasonable distance of the central post office. We can hardly be expected to build a new post office at an expense of $50,000 in every municipality which is brought into the city.
What is the revenue from the present Maisonneuve post office for which we are paying a rent of $60 a year?

Revenue last year $5,515, money orders issued $22,492, money orders paid $12,308. In pursuance of the plan adopted by the Post Office Department this will become a postal station. If I am not mistaken there are three postal stations in the city of Toronto.
They did not cost $50,000 each?

I think one of them cost more than that. Maisonneuve is practically in the centre of the city of Montreal, because considerable territory to the east has recently been taken in. but Maisonneuve is a long way from the Montreal central post office. It is essential for the accommodation of this very rapidly growing municipality that it should have suitable postal accommodation.

Maisonneuve is in the eastern portion of the city and you have a vote also in the estimates for an eastern postal station, so that I presume the two would be in close proximity. How many post offices will Montreal have in the near future if you keep multiplying them in that way?

These different postal stations are regarded by the Post Office Department as necessary for the public accommodation. There is one station called the St. Catherine West station, one called the eastern postal station, one called the Point St. Charles postal station, .and there will also be the Westmount postal station. The hon. gentleman must Temember that Montreal has doubled its population in the last ten years and there are half a million people in the city now. It is spread over a

great extent of territory, and any gentleman who is familiar with Montreal will agree that these postal stations are absolutely essential.
Is there free mail delivery from these stations?
I do not know as to Maisonneuve, but there is in Montreal.
How far is the Maisonneuve postal station from the eastern postal station?
About three miles from the central station.
But how far is the eastern station from the Maisonneuve station?

It is about three miles also. Along the river it is three miles from Maisonneuve to the central post office, but the eastern station Is situated north on St. Catherine street so that geographically it would also be about three miles from Maisonneuve.
How many postal stations will you have in Montreal altogether?

I do not know that any one could tell that unless the Postmaster General were asked to give the official figures, because there are a great many post offices in the annexed territory. There is one at Bordeaux, one at Ahuntsic, probably four in Longue Pointe, one at Parc Terminal, one at the Lakefield Cement factory and one at Tetreauville. When I was a candidate in 1902 there were only a couple of electors in Tetreauville, but in 1908 it had a population of 1,600. At Parc Terminal there were only 12 voters in 1908, but there are more than 150 there now. The deputy Postmaster General is studying the newly annexed territory in order to see what improvements can be made.
M<r. SPROULE, The hon. gentleman from Laval misunderstands me. I have no desire to refuse all necessary postal accommodation to the people of the city of Montreal, and the newly annexed districts, but I am trying to ascertain if I can get some approximate estimate of what the post office service in Montreal will cost and whether the government are following a business policy or not in this respect. The hon. gentleman mixes up post offices and postal stations, but there is a great difference between them. There are a lot of post offices kept by business establishments, such as drug stores, which do not cost much comparatively speaking. But take the eastern postal station for which we voted $40,000 last year, I presume that will not finish it. Then there is the Maisonneuve post office and I do not know how many more. Sure-Mr. PUGSLEY.
ly some one ought to be able to tell the House how many there are in the city of Montreal of these postal stations and post offices for which the country is paying so much.

There is one on St. 'Catherine street west which cost about '$75,000. Then there is one on St. Catherine street east, the eastern postal station, which will cost in the vicinity of $75,000. Then there is one we are providing for Maisonneuve, which will cost in the vicinity of $35,000, besides $8,437 for the site. Then parliament has granted a vote for a public building at Westmount, which is a separate municipality, and the plans for which are being prepared. It is estimated that the Westmount building will co3t $75,000 in addition to the site. Then there is a postal station at Point St. Charles, which cost in the vicinity of $50,000.
What does the general post office cost ?

The total cost is in the vicinity of a million dollars, perhaps more. Lately a very large addition was made by building on the site of the ' Gazette ' establishment running through to Craig street. We are besides, remodelling the old building so as to make it as nearly fire proof as possible.
What is there in Ste. Cunegonde ?
That was built before the annexation of Ste. Cunegonde to the city. Ste. Cunegonde was a separate municipality.
That building is not owned by the government. The post office department rents quarters in it.
When did the department first decide to purchase this site for a post office ?
Authority was given the minister on the 22nd December last.
When were the other sites purchased ?
After the first site was purchased, we decided, on the 22nd of December last, to make an exchange.
Did the suggestion come from the department or the vendor ?

It came first from the hon. member for Maisonneuve. Then Mr. Morgan offered to make the exchange. We had die offer looked into by an expert of the department who reported that the land we would get in exchange would be of considerably greater value than the one given up and the site was much more desirable.
So that here we have a private individual giving in exchange to the government a much more valuable property than the one he obtained in return.

Mr. James Morgan has a considerable quantity of land in that vicinity and is laying out a square with the idea of beautifying it and rendering more valuable the surrounding property, which he owns there; and he said that in order to have the post office situated on a spacious piece of ground, so that it would be more striking from a public standpoint, he was willing to make the exchange although giving up a larger and more valuable area.
When the selection was made in the first place, was it made because the site first chosen was the best lor a post office ?
Yes, it is right along side the other.
But in view of the fact that another gentleman would benefit by the change, the department agreed to accommodate him.
In our opinion, the site offered in exchange was a better one.
And the hon. minister knows that the gentleman in question, Mr. Morgan, is a Liberal ?
I do not know it.
I am asking the minister for the information.
My information is that he is a very staunch Conservative.
Does the hon. minister know that of his own personal knowledge ?
I have been informed on most reliable authority that he is.

Might I ask if the
information came from the hon. member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Verville) ?
No.
Did he Tecommend it ?

Yes, and it was also recommended by an expert of the department, who has had very large experience in examining and valuing properties and on whose judgment we rely. He recommended this exchange on the grounds that it was very desirable from a public standpoint.

Was he the same
gentleman who recommended the purchase of the first site ?
Yes.
Then his	judgement in the first instance was wrong ?
Not at all.
But in the second instance, his opinion would benefit somebody else.
We are getting a decidedly better site for the same money.
We have the right to assume that in the first instance the minister did not do so well as he might have done anu that in the second the /change was made to benefit a private individual.
All I can do is to deny that absolutely and to state that the facts are entirely different.
The hon. gentleman said it was changed because the individual said he had a plot of land there, and to place a post office there would benefit him.

No ; my hon. friend asked me if I could conceive what would be his motive in giving to the Crown a more valuable piece of land, and 1 mentioned that, as he had more land there, and proposed to lay out a public square, he might be influenced by that. But, so far as I had knowledge, and, I believe, so far as the officials of the department had knowledge, to get the larger area after we had purchased the smaller one, we would have to pay a larger sum of money. We bought land which we thought would be suitable, paying the lowest possible price. Afterwards, we had tire opportunity of making the exchange for a larger area equally well situated-in some respects better situated, because it either actually forms a part of or is immediately adjacent to a public square.
But the change would never have been made if the property had not been in possession of a Liberal.
The deputy minister informs me that, in the exchange, we get a whole block of land in place of the smaller area.
What size?
I gave the figures-100 feet by 125 feet.
What is to be the total cost of the building including fixtures?
The instructions to the chief architect were not to exceed $35,000. That would be without the postal fittings but would include heating and wiring for electric light.
Have plans been prepared?
No.
Upon what are the estimates based?

In view of the size of Maisonneuve -and the cost of other postal stations, I felt 1 was justified in saying to the chief architect that ih 3 must not exceed $35,000, and he will prepare his plans accordingly.
The minister knows that such instructions have been given and yet the buildings have cost from twenty-five to fifty per cent more. Has he any guarantee that this will not occur in this case?
The hon. gentleman has the guarantee. He may decline to take it.
It is only worth what the experience of the past proves such things to be worth.
Exactly, but you can't get any more than that.
I observe that the minister said, a year ago last November, that he would give the same instructions. Has anything been done to carry out the instructions and prepare the plans?
Yes, and we are getting very good buildings at a lower cost than was formerly paid for buildings in places of equal population.
With the assistance of the hon. member for Laval (Mr. C. A. Wilson), can the minister tell whether there is a street postal delivery in Maisonneuve?

I would not state it as a fact, but I believe there is. If there is not free delivery at this moment, there will be in the near future, because the districts adjoining Maisonneuve and recently annexed to Montreal are claiming free delivery, and it is to be organized. That is the reason I support the item ; you cannot erect a decent building suitable for the needs of that portion of Montreal-for this really forms part of the city, and I presume this building will be a very important centre of distribution-at a lower expense.

Where there is a street delivery, you do not need as expensive a post office building as though there were no delivery. And, considering that the post office has been carried on in this place in a building rented at $5 a month, does the minister think he is justified in expending $50,000- for, with the cost of fittings and so on, it Is pretty sure to cost that amount-which would mean a cost of Mr. PUGSLEY.
$5,000 a year as compared with the $60 a year formerly paid.

If I thought Maisonneuve was going to be a place of not more than four or five thousand people within the next ten or twenty years, I ijhould say we ought not to have a building costing more than $15,000 or $20,000. But Maisonneuve is bound to grow. I am satisfied from what I have heard about it that it is not too much to look forward to an increase in population within fifteen years to fifty thousand at least to be served by this postal station. It is like the West. Take the city of Lethbridge, in the constituency of my hon. friend from Medicine Hat (Mr. Magrath). It has a population of 13,000 or 14,000 to-day. But there is reason to believe that in ten years it will have a population of 35,000, and in twenty years perhaps 50,000. In erecting public buildings, I must look to the future. In Lethbridge, we have agreed to pay $30,000 for a site for a public building. And when I ask for an appropriation for the erection of a. build-I think I shall be obliged to state that the building will cost $50,000 or $60,000, perhaps even more. We are building, not for to-morrow, or for next year, or even for the next five years, but for the next quarter-century or half-century, and wh^re a citv is growing rapidly, we must endeavour to meet the requirements of that city as it is to be. In Maisonneuve, the people are suffering for want of postal accommodation, and I feel it would not be reasonable or proper to go on with the limited *and miserable accommodation of the present.
Mr. P^BLEY. I am sure the minister (Mr. Pugsley) wants to be fair about this matter. Will he tell us how much money is spent on one of these postal stations in Montreal as a rule? What is the average cost of a postal station?

I gave the items to the committee a little while ago. The cost of th" eastern postal station will be about $<'5,000, the cost of the Westmount station will be about the same. The cost of the one at Maisonneuve we expect will not exceed $35,000.

The minister gave us the same estimate as he did last year with regard to the cost. In making that calculation, I would like to ask him if he has taken into account the fact that the member for that riding has an eight-hour day Bill before this House, and expects it to pass. When it has passed and is applied to the erection of public buildings, has the minister, in making up his estimates, taken the fact into account that the passage of that Bill will mean a reduction of one-fifth in the number of hours the men will labour?

I have not given special attention to that point. But if it should result in shortening the hours of labour a little bit, even though the work might cost a little more, I should be very glad. But I do not anticipate that it will cost much more in consequence of an eight-hour day Act. Perhaps by reason of the short hours the men will work more rapidly and put in better work.

I do not think that the hard-headed business men of this country will have much respect for a minister who would leave such a fact out of account in making up his estimates. What this House wants is an estimate that will be approximately correct, and if you take a building which will require five hundred hours of labour to erect, and that labour is charged at the common price for every ten hours, say $2 a day, and if you reduce the time by one-fifth, then, .to say that it is not going to cost much more, as the hon. gentleman does, will not increase the respect of the public for his intelligence.
How does the hon. gentleman make it one-fifth?
Two hours cut off ten hours is one-fifth.
In Montreal labourers do not work ten hours now.
That is approximately a day's work over the country.
Not in the city of Montreal.
I don't know w7hat it is in Montreal, but that is what it is in the city of Toronto.
I do not think in the building trade anywhere it is more than nine hours a day on the average.

In my part of the country, both in town and city, the average day ox labour is ten hours, and I am speaking on that basis when I refer to these buildings in Montreal. I do not know whether it applies to the city of Montreal, but it d( es apply to the country as a whole.

When my hon. friend says that we shall lose two hours a day iron', the labour of every man who works on this building at Maisonneuve, because if this Bill passes they will only be obliged to work eight hours a day, my hon. friend will see, when I tell him that at the present time in the building trade a working day is nine hours in the city of Montreal, he is just one hundred per cent out of the way. New, I do not think that the passage of this Bill will make much difference, at all events I have not calculated the difference. These figures are based upon a nine-hour day. When this Bill passes I suppose the chief architect will revise his estimates.

I may tell the minister that I do know something about the construction of buildings, because I have been an employer of labour for the last forty years, and have been in the building trade for a length of time. Montreal is a great city and should have all the accommodation a city of its size would naturally require. I am not personally objecting to any expenditure that is needed in Montreal, . but the question is whether it is necessary for the convenience or service of the people to have, first, a central post office building at an expense of over a million dollars, and then no less than five other post offices at an expense of $318,000. It seems to me that while you might properly have postal stations for your work conjointly with the post office in the distribution and gathering of postal matter, the postal stations would not require to be so expensive and they could be supplied very cheaply. I know that some of our stations in Toronto are supplied very cheaply. I do not know the exact amount, but I believe that there they are comparatively cheap when put alongside these Montreal stations. Does Montreal require an expensive central post office, and then in addition five or six other post offices? If you have these are you not then making it confusing to those who are making use of these post offices in regard to addressing letters? Suppose you are addressing letters to Maisonneuve, it would be to Maisonneuve, but it is in the city of Montreal, and in addition you have the eastern postal station, and how would you distinguish that from the western postal station?
Montreal east.
Montreal east. What is the other one?-Westmount. That would be addressed, I suppose, 'Westmount'?
' Westmount,' yes.

It seems to me that all this would be confusing. If you address a letter to the city of Toronto you address it, of course to a certain street and number, but to the general post office always. How do you manage it in Montreal, and will these different post offices make any difference in addressing letters to or from them so as to be sure of them reaching their destinations?
My hon. friend knows how it is managed in the city of London where they have London North, London West, London East, and London South.

I am not at all sure that as regards the delivery of letters the same principle applies in Montreal as in London. If it did I could understand that probably it would work all right. But it

seems to me that there is no need of these expensive post offices in addition to the central office. Might you not have small distributing offices at little cost to the country for collecting and distributing the mail in connection with the central post office? You have the free mail delivery as well. Why it should require so much to provide accommodation for the mail service of Montreal, which has a population of about half a million people when, in the city of Toronto, which has a very, much smaller population, but returns nearly double the amount of revenue to the country, it does not cost perhaps half the amount, is something that I cannot understand. Does it not suggest there is something wrong in the plan upon which the work is laid out, or the business principle that is carried into effect in connection with these various post offices?
I do not know as to Toronto, but I rather assume that there is a post office at North Toronto; is there not?
No; there is a postal station.
Does the hon. gentleman know the corner of Charles and Yonge streets in Toronto? There is a postal station which cost $95,000.
I know something about it, but I am not very familiar with it.
There are these two.
What is the revenue from them?
It is not a question of revenue; it is a question of the necessity of having these postal stations for the accommodation of the people. There is another at Parkdale.
Yes, but the mail goes through the central office.
Have you not a building there?
Not that I know of; I would not say that there is not.
Yes, I am told that there is a postal station at Parkdale, but the point I want to make is that postal stations exist in Toronto on identically the same plan as in Montreal.

What did the one at
Parkdale cost?
An hon. MEMBEE. Let it go.
All right, we will let it go.

But that is not an answer. If the city of Toronto, with about Mr. SPROULE.
400,000 people, returns double the postal revenue, and if that number of people seem to be well served and the cost of providing the accommodation is less than half of what it is in Montreal, do not you think there is something wrong in the principle we follow in serving the people of Montreal as compared with that adopted in Toronto? It seems to me that there must be of necessity, and if it costs so much more to handle millions less of letters and papers in one city than it does in the other and returns to the revenue only half as much, I think it might to be remodelled in some way, because there is a want of good business principle involved in it. .

I do not know as to the revenue, but it may veTy well be that those large departmental stores that you have in Toronto, such as the Eatons, whose business amounts to millions-perhaps to a million dollars a month-and whose business is largely done through the mails, the Simpsons and the other big departmental stores, would add immensely to the volume of the postal business and that could easily be transacted with one office, because the mail matter could all be put in bags and removed from these stores. As my hon. friend referred to Toronto, I mention these postal stations to show that the same plan is adopted in Toronto as in Montreal, and that postal stations are necessary for the public accommodation. My bon. friend representing the city -of St. John (Mr. Daniel) knows that we have postal stations in that city, that we have St. John North, St. John West and St. John East, St. John East being where the main post office is and St. John West being the place at which a public building was erected a good many years ago for postal purposes. London is divided into districts, there is no inconvenience, and I presume that in Montreal it would be the same. It may be Montreal East, Montreal West, or Montreal South, according as these postal stations may be denominated.

Then I would like if the minister, at some future stage in his estimates, when we are dealing with public buildings, would give us information as to how many stations there are in Toronto, the cost of them to the country and how many there are in Montreal.

Would my hon. friend be good enough to let that stand until the postal estimates are under consideration, because it would properly be furnished by the Post Office Department. If he would mention it then I will see that he gets the information.

Then I may be told by the Postmaster General that it is not in his department, but in that of the Department

of Public Works, and I am asking the Minister of Public Works to provide that informa'tion at some future time, when we are dealing with his estimates again.
Mr. PUGSLEY'. I will see that it is furnished.	,
Marieville public building, $17,000.
Of this amount $10,000 is a revote.
What is this building to cost?

The contract price is $16,300. In addition to that we paid $1,500 for the site; survey .of site, legal and travelling expenses, $340.91; fittings, furniture, lock boxes estimated at $3,500; sidewalks, fences, contingencies and superintendence, which will be in addition to the contract pi ice of $16,300.

For the two places to be served it would be about 2,400.

The parish of Ste. Marie de Monnoir is served by the post office of the city of Marieville and according to the census taken nine years ago the population of the parish is 1,036. That population has been increasing since. I live pretty near Marieville and I know that its population has largely increased in the last nine years. The statement read by the minister did not mention the two railways which run through the city of Marieville. Marieville is the chief town of the riding, it contains the registry office, a classical college, and among many others a very important factory under the management and ownership of Mr. Guillet. I may add that according to the provincial statistics 54
the riding of Rouville as well as the riding of St. Hyacinthe which I have the honour to represent, are at the head of the list so far as public instruction is concerned.
Is there any other post office in the parish of Ste. Marie de Monnoir?
I do not know of any.
Do you know there are not any others?
I do not think there are, the parish is small in territory but thickly populated.

It would be extraordinary if a parish of that population had only one post office. These parishes usually have two or three post offices, and if the hon. gentleman states it is a fact that to his knowledge there is only one post office for the town and the parish I must accept itA but it is a very extraordinary thing.

It is not so very extraordinary, because in St. Vincent de Paul with a population of 1,012 in the village, and 1,500 in the parish, according to the census of 1901, there is only one post office, the same applies to the parishes on Isle Gesu as my hon. friend knows, and it is pretty nearly the same thing in every village and parish in Quebec.
No.
Well, perhaps they are not so progressive as we are in Lachute.
Is a parish in Quebec something similar to a township in Ontario?
I am not familiar with the topography of a township in Ontario, but I do know what a parish in Quebec is.
How many miles square?
St. Vincent de Paul is nine miles long by six miles wide, but it is not square. If my hon. friend is strong in geometry he can make the calculation, it is a triangular.
Will the minister tell me what is the size of the parish of Ste. Marie de Monnoir? .

I cannot say, I can inform my hon. friend that there was a memorandum filed by the Minister of Marine and Fisheries which contained a statement from the mayor of Marieville that according to a municipal census taken some time ago the population of the town was 1,671, that it had since increased to 1,750, and that there were 250 students in the college making the population of the village 2,000.
Wliat is the population of the parish?
1,054, making the population of town and parish 3,054.
Are we "to understand that this post office is the sole post office for the parish and the village?
That is the information I have.

Of course, you may get a population of 2,400 into a very small space or you may have it widely scattered so that some of the residents would have to go five or six miles for their mail. In that view it is important that we should know the size of the parish. I would also like to ask the minister, on whose recommendation this post office is being established. Are we to understand that the Postmaster General has asked for a post office there?
The application was made by the board of trade of the town of Marieville.
Has it the approval of the Postmaster General?

I do not know. I may say that the Postmaster General is not in the habit of either approving or disapproving of the erection of buildings for post office and customs services. This is a matter in regard to which the Public Works Department has to take the responsibility. In this particular case the application was made by the board of trade and was strongly supported by my colleague the Minister of Marine and Fisheries.

Am I to understand from the Minister of Public Works that in regard to the erection of post offices the Postmaster General is not consulted and is not in the habit of saying anything one way or the other? I can hardly believe my ears. If that is the case, it strikes me as one of the most extraordinary things I have ever heard since I have been in this House.

I may say that I have felt myself that it would be very desirable if the Post Office Department would pass upon the applications. Petitions have been sent to the Post Office Department, and the view that department has taken has been that as it has never been the practice, I suiipose running back to confederation, for the Post Office Department to pass upon the question of erecting a public building at a particular place, they did not express an opinion. Lately we have been urging strongly that the Post Office Department should pass upon the applications and my deputy tells me that just recently in regard to one application that department has ex-

piessed an opinion, and we are in hopes that the request which my department has made will be favourably received by the Post Office Department. Of course, we always get them to approve of the plans when we propose to proceed with the erection of a building.
In what constituency is this?
Rouville.
Who represents it?
The Minister of Marine and Fisheries.

The statement now made by the hon. minister gives us the reason why so many of these buildings are being built contrary to the public interest. If the Post Office Department found they had need of a building in a particular place, and made a request to the Minister of Public Works to furnish it, they would have some regard to the size of the place and the revenue it yielded, and try to get a building suitable to the requirements of the service. This Marieville post office is another sample of a public building being erected where it is not required, and on a too extravagant scale. There are many places throughout Canada far larger than this and with a far larger revenue which have no public buildings,' and when my hon. friend from Laval tells me there are paiishes in Quebec which have only one post office, and my hon. friend from St. Hyacinthe tells me this is one of the parishes, I will not dispute the fact, but that- very fact is a reason why this post office should not be built. In my county there is no parish w'ith only one post office, and this parish of Ste. Marie de Monnoir, if it is an ordinary sized parish, ought to have more than one post office. Now, you are proposing to spend $25,000 for a public building in this small village, which will cost the country for ever 4 per cent on the money, or $1,000 a year. The government would do much, better if they would spend that $1,000 a year in providing a couple mere post offices in this parish and establishing a postal route so that the people vr< uld have their mail delivered where they live. Of what use is it to spend this money and compel the people to go 5 or 6 miles for their mail? This government ought to be ashamed to spend money in this way.

I do not want to be understood as giving any factious opposition to this item, but when these post office items are brought up I think the Postmaster General should be here. I will teli you why I feel it my duty to my constituents to enter my protest against this item. There is one township in the county I have the honour to represent where there

is not a single post office, and the people have to go from 9 to 14 miles for their mail. Last year I made an application to, the Postmaster General to establish a post office in a certain part of my county where there were some 22 families, with their nearest post office from 5 to 8 miles distant. They sent a petition asking for a bi-weekly service. The cost of that would be $70 a year, with $35 a year for the postmaster's salary. The answer I received from the Postmaster General was that as it would cost that much to provide such a service, while the revenue would not probably be more than $10 or $15 a year, he did not feel warranted in making the expenditure. These people may walk from 5 to 8 miles for their mail because this government cannot afford to spend something like $90 a year in giving them a service twice a week. While I have no objection to large cities like Montreal having a more frequent service than country places, there is any amount of evidence in the estimates as they come down here from year to year that the country districts are grossly neglected as compared with the smaller cities and towns.
I repeat that that is not a fair condition of things. Let me give you another Instance to -show how unfairly this matter "works out. I asked for a post office on the border of the city of Kingston, just on the edge between the border of the city and the adjoining township. There is a school house within a few yards of the proposed site of the post office. There are stores right convenient, there is a regular mail route which goes down that street, the main street of the city, past this point where I asked for a new post office, so that it would cost nothing more to carry the mails there. The city is. served by letter carriers right up to the border of which I have spoken, but the good people there, when they want their mails, have to go to a sub-post office in the city about three quarters of a mile from this point. What would it cost to .give accommodation to the people in that district ? Simply $35 a year, the postmaster's salary It would not cost even that much because there would be some revenue from the office, so that the total cost would be only a matter of some $10 or $20 a year. Why (cannot the people then have this postal accommodation ? Why are they deprived bf their evident and just rights in this respect ? I cannot understand why. I find in these estimates item after item of $15,000 and $20,000 for post offices in insignificant places, and we are told that the Postmaster General knows nothing about them, that he is not even consulted. That is not only very strange, but absolutely unjustifiable.

While we are considering the appropriations for post offices which the government propose to build in a number of little places, there is a case I have in mind of quite a different .character which I desire to submit to the hon. minister. I would at the outset assure my hon. friend that I do not intend offering any criticism which will in any way affect that hilarity he thinks is so necessary in order that he may pass his estimates through this House. What I desire to impress on the hon. minister is the very urgent necessity for a public building in the town of Walkerville, one of the leading towns in the province of Ontario. The minister will remember that last winter I called upon him personally and had an interview with him regarding the construction of a public building at this point. For the very courteous manner in which he received me, I have nothing but the kindest words to say. I left his office with a very light heart indeed, feeling that I had accomplished something and that possibly I had learned something as well. I actually felt that by going down to the minister and submitting to him personally the plain unvarnished facts, he would possibly give to my request a favourable consideration, which he might not give if I were to rise in this House and criticise the government because it had not done its duty to the people at this particular point. You can imagine then my astonishment when I read the estimates this year. I had to rub my eyes to see whether I was asleep or not when I found that there Was not one cent in them for the construction of a building which my hon. friend had promised he would provide in order to meet the needs and requirements of the town of Walkerville. While the House has been considering the estimates these past few days, I took occasion to look up a number of the towns in which the government have deemed it wise to construct public buildings. I went through the lists in the provinces of Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island and Quebec, and I do not rise to offer one word of criticism upon any of the appropriations made for these places, but simply to point out that by no stretch of reason can it be considered fair to give small towns, with a population of not 1,000 people and with a revenue in one case of only $660, expensive public buildings and neglect, an important town like that of Walkerville with a postal revenue last year of over $12,000, although it has been repeatedly applying to this government for just treatment in this regard. Take, for instance, the town of Tis-nish, with a revenue of $988 and a customs duties of $2,141, we have an appropriation of $14,000 for a post office in that hamlet. Mind you, Mr. Chairman, I am not passing a word of criticism on that ex-

penditure. Take Fairville with a postal revenue of $1,191 and no customs collection, it is to be endowed with a $15,000 post office. Grand Falls had a revenue in 1909-10 of $3,118 and no customs collections, yet it is considered entitled to a $15,000 post office. Hampton, which had a postal revenue collected in 1909-10 of $660 and has no customs collections, is given $3,000 for a post office. Hartland, where the postal revenue is $1,955 and the customs collections nil, is given a $15,000 post office. Hillsborough, with $1,900 revenue and $11,612 customs collections, is also to he given a $15,000 post office. In all these towns the population runs from 700 and in not one of them does it reach 3,000. Now take the town of Walkerville and contrast it with these. It seems to me that these facts are sufficient to prove that this important town is worthy of consideration at the hands of this or any other government. Its board of trade has been agitating this matter for a number of years. It surely cannot be said with any degree of accuracy that the reason that Walkerville has been neglected is that a Liberal-Conservative - represents the riding. For twenty-one years that riding was true to the Liberal party of Canada, and if the political affiliations of the representative was the determining factor, even men the government has been derelict in its duty toward Walkerville. I have taken a great interest in trying to secure justice for that town as well as for every other part of the riding. And, while I am anxious that justice shall be done to that riding, I am anxious also that justice shall be done to every part of this country. The Minister of Public Works stated a little while ago that the first thing >he considers in deciding whether any particular place shall be given a post office building is whether good accommodation is already provided either by private means or otherwise. I submit to the minister that there is not sufficient accommodation provided to meet the needs and requirements of Walkerville to-day. I was informed by the manager of the Home Bank only last week that the people to-day have to wait three hours before the mail is distributed in the town of Walkerville. That in itself is sufficient, it seems to me, to prove that something should be done for that important town. A statement was

made on the floor of this House this afternoon to the effect that the governmmt did not give the riding represented by members of the opposition their fair appropriations. I have not been in this House a sufficient length of time to enable me to say whether that is so or not. But I submit for the consideration of the government this plain fact, that this great country in which we live belongs to the Canadian people. It does not belong to the particular party that happens to govern the country at any particular time. I believe this country stands to the Canadian people as an asset, the people thereof are the beneficiaries of that asset, and the government thereof are the trustees of that asset during the period it is the pleasure of the people to leave them in office. I say that these appropriations should be made to the different ridings upon a certain basis, having regard only for the development of the country and the just rsquirements of its various sections. I desire to say to my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works that I am not in the least criticising the government, I am only pleading with him to do justice to the town of Walkerville, and to give them that measure of relief to which they are justly entitled in respect to a public building.

I think we must all admire the spirit in which my hon. friend has spoken. The hon. gentleman has only done what it was proper for him to do in the interest of his constituency, in calling my attention, as head of the department, to the needs of Walkerville in respect to a public building. But let me say to my hon. friend when he finds fault with me, that if I were to place in the estimates a sufficient amount to meet what I think are the reasonable requirements of the various sections of this country, even my hon. friend would be appalled at the magnitude of the figures. We have to cut our garment according to our cloth; we have to consider the various requests which are made, and to apportion to each the amount the Minister of Finance will allow us to expend according to our judgment from time to time. Now, I am not one of those who believe, like some hon. gentlemen opposite, that we can justify the expenditure of hundreds of thousands and millions of dollars in the great cities of Canada, while neglecting the erection of public buildings in the towns! and smaller cities. I am a great believer in giving encouragement to the people of the towns and smaller cities, so far as we can reasonably do so. But to-day, all parts of Canada are growing so rapidly, towns and cities are springing up so fast, particularly in the western provinces, and are growing so rapidly, that it is impossible for the Department of Public Works to keep pace with all the requirements. Now, I may
say with regard to Walkerville, that I was glad to have my hon. friend come and see me. We talked over the requirements of the town, and I was pleased to be able to tell him that I am in favour of constructing a public building in Walkerville. 1 told him that, I tell him that tonight. More than that, I can tell my hon. friend that for the purpose of erecting a public building in the town of Walkerville, we have bought one of the prettiest and most convenient sites which can be obtained in that rising town, and I intend at a not distant date to submit for the consideration of my colleagues the placing in the estimates of an amount to supplement what we have already done, by the construction of a handsome public building upon the site we have purchased.
Where is the site, and when was it bought?
My hon. friend will find it in the Auditor General's Report for the year 1908-9. We paid some $5,000 for the site.
What month, please?
The account does not give the month.

I appreciate the kind words in which the minister has referred to the application I made to his department. I may say that it is immaterial to me whether the site was bought before the last election or since. What I am concerned about is to obtain justice for that very important town in my constituency. The impression I had from the minister when I interviewed him last winter, was that the demands upon his department had been much greater last year than he expected, but that he would place in the estimates a sufficient sum to erect a suitable public building in the town of Walkerville. But when I consulted the main estimates and found therein no vote for Walkerville, my hope was dashed to the ground.

On this side of the House we do not raise objection to any reasonable expenditures for public buildings in any part of this country, but we object to the way the allocation of public money is made. There are many towns in this country that need a public building far more than the town of Marieville. I would move that this vote be reduced from $17,000 to $10,000.

My hon. friend surely cannot be serious. The time to move for a reduction of this vote was when we asked for it in the first instance. But my hon. friend did not then seek to make a reduction. Having obtained the vote, we pro-

ceeded to enter into a contract in good faith under the authority of parliament, and surely my hon. friend will see that this is not the time to make a motion of this character. I presume my hon. friend does not make the motion without some serious expectation of carrying it, and if it were carried he sees the awkward position in which it would place the government. Suppose he were president of a company, or trustee for a company, and the shareholders of that company had invested him with authority to undertake a certain work and to sign contracts; and then, at the next meeting, a shareholder said: Oh, we think you made a mistake, and we are going to refuse to give you the money which will enable you to carry out in good faith the contract you have entered into, what would my hon. friend think of those whom he represented under those circumstances? We have entered into a contract in good faith, invited public tenders under the authority of parliament, and pursuant to the appropriation which parliament granted.
Why then does my hon. friend take up Marieville? Why does he let votes pass for other public buildings? Why does he allow the vote to pass for various buildings in Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick without challenging the merits of the case in so far as asking for a vote from the committee is concerned, while when it comes down to Marieville, he asks this committee to put the Department of Public Works in such a position that it cannot carry out the contract it has entered into by the authority of parliament? Is it because that constituency is represented by my colleague the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Brodeur)? Surely my hon. friend, with his breadth of view, would not be influenced by considerations like that. I do not think that my hon. friend would. Therefore, it is that I am surprised that to-night my hon. friemd should single out this one town in the province of Quebec and seek to prevent us from carrying out in good faith contracts w'hich we have entered into in pursuance of the authority of parliament. It does seem to me that my hon. friend, upon consideration, will feel that he is not doing justice to the town of Marieville and I would be very sorry indeed to think, although it looks very much like it, that my hon. friend has picked out this particular towm because it is in the constituency represented by my colleague the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Brodeur). The time is not tonight to refuse this vote unless my hon. friend can show that we do not need it in order to pay the contractor who is erecting this building. The time was when we asked for this vote in the first instance. That is the time when objection should have been taken, because, if then my hon. friend could Mr. PUGSLEY.
have succeeded in persuading the committee not to grant the vote, of course, we would not have entered into a contract, but having entered into the contract on the good faith of parliament, my hon. friend will see that, if his view should prevail before this committee, a gross injustice would be done.

In the first place the question of the representative of this constituency has nothing to do with the matter at all. The minister must be troubled by his conscience or he would not raise that question at all at this juncture. Nobody else would suggest that we had singled out this item for that reason and there are lots of other items that we might call a vote on equally with this. Last night we objected very strongly to some items that were brought up in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick and for exactly the same reason. The minister said: You do not take any votes, why do you not challenge us to a vote? To-night we take the first item of this nature in order to challenge a vote and we say, to show that we are acting in good faith in this matter, that we will move to reduce this amount, so that the minister cannot find any fault with us for not challenging him to a vote. He says: How can you have a board of directors first giving authority to carry on certain work and the next time there is a meeting of shareholders they change their minds and say that they will not proceed with this work? That is not the position here to-day. We are not asking to alter the vote of last year, the vote under which the minister is acting, and the only vote under which he has authority to act. He came to this House last year and told us how much money he required, we voted it and he has only the right to spend that money in accordance with that vote. He comes and says that this is not the time to challenge this item. We say that this is a public building on which he is spending too much money, that it is far bigger than there is any need of, that there is no reason why it should not be made smaller. The minister says that we did not challenge a vote last year? There the minister makes a statement that he is not sure of. He will make any statement apparently which will answer his purpose for the time being. As a matter of fact we did challenge this item last year, and did take a vote on it. It was because, in looking up ' Hansard ' last year, that I noticed we had taken a vote on this item, that I thought it was probably only right that we should vote on the same item tonight so that the minister could not say that we had not challenged this vote at the right time. Therefore, Mr. Chairman, it seems to me that the minister has not very much ground for saying that it is not fair and right for us to take a vote on this matter to-night. If the amount is reduced it

-simply means that the minister will have to put up a sjnaller building without so many of the etceteras.

I think I must be right in this: that at the last session of parliament, when this vote was first asked, I stated substantially what the building would cost, and my hon. friend knows perfectly well that the vote was not given for the entire completion of the building. What I say is that when a minister states what a building is going to cost and parliament makes an appropriation for a portion of the cost to enable the work of construction to go on during the current year, the faith of parliament is committed to providing the balance of the money that is necessary to complete the building. My hon. friend cannot be serious to-night in making this motion at a time when the work is under construction and when +v'is money is required to pay the contractor. My hon. friend says that if the amendment carried the only result would be that I would have to erect a smaller building. That would be true if nothing had been done, if no work had been performed, but the work has been entered upon, and what my hon. friend suggests cannot now be done. What I say is that, parliament having passed a vote for the purpose, it would be a breach of faith now with the contractors to make a reduction in this vote, because it is too late to alter the contract or the character of the building. Now my hon. friend did not give me the page of ' Hansard.' He sent the book over to me with a page open, but I do not see upon the page which he sent me that the Marieville public building is referred to.
